2 
 
CHAPTER-I 
 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS WHICH HAVE BEEN ACCEPTED 
BY THE MINISTRY 
ANNUAL PLAN 2019-20 
Recommendation/Observation 
1.  The Committee recommends that the Ministry should strive for optimum utilization of 
the funds by spreading the utilization across all the quarters of the financial year so as to 
ensure quality in the projects as well as  adherence to the guidelines of the Ministry of 
Finance issued in this regard. 
(Para 14) 
Reply of the Ministry 
1.1     Observations of the Committee have been noted for needful compliance. 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
2.  The Committee takes note of the major activities/initiatives undertaken by the Ministry 
during the year 2019 -20. The Committee hopes these activities/initiatives will be carried 
on with the same pace and vigour in the year 2020-21. 
(Para 31) 
Reply of the Ministry 
2.1     The observations of the Committee are noted.  
 
OUTLAY 2020-21: Demands vis-à-vis Allocations 
Recommendation/Observation 
3.  The Committee notes that the gap between the projected requirement of the Ministry 
and the amount allocated by the Ministry of Finance has further widened to about 40% of 
the projected requirement at BE stage in 2020 -21, as against a gap of 34.5% and 22.5% 
at RE stage in 2018 -19 and 2019-20 respectively. The Committee hopes that the Ministry 
of Road Transport and Highways is able to carry out its pro jects and schemes by 
considering the inter -se priorities of its projects. The Committee recommends that the 
Ministry should strive to ensure that the quality of the Ministry’s projects is not 
compromised due to availability of limited funds. 
(Para 34) 
Reply of the Ministry 
3.1     The concerns of the Committee are noted. All efforts shall  be made to ensure that 
quality of implementation of projects is not compromised. Further, additional fund 
requirements, if any, shall be appropriately projected under RE 2020-21. 

3 
 
 
ROAD DEVELOPMENT 
Recommendation/Observation 
4.  The Committee is of the view that the efficiency of Highway alignment in Greenfield 
projects is much higher than Brownfield projects. The Committee recommends that as per 
the policy of MoRTH, linear road construction and Greenfield projects should be 
accorded utmost priority for construction of road projects. 
(Para 41) 
Reply of the Ministry 
4.1     Majority of the existing Road projects have been developed in the past with 
connectivity of enroute towns as the key consideration. This has led to sub -optimal 
alignments, involving longer routes to be covered between major destinations. Longer 
the route, h igher is the cost and time involved in traversing the length of the Highway, 
which also entails associated environmental costs. There is a feasibility of completely 
new alignments, following crow -flight concept to the extent feasible, which reduces the 
distance between two major connectivity (Origin and Destination) points. The Ministry 
has issued guidelines dated 26.02.2018 for the DPR Consultants in this regard.  
4.2    Under Phase -I of Bharatmala Pariyojana, about 5,871 km length of Greenfield 
corridors have been identified for development. Out of these , projects in about 1,645 km 
have been awarded. Balance lengths are targeted to be awarded by FY 2021 -22.   
 
Recommendation/Observation 
5.  The Committee recommends that the Ministry should ensure the inclusion of provision 
for service roads on both sides across the National Highways network. The Committee 
feels that important roads with significant traffic load, such as Hyderabad -Kurnool 
Tollgate to Bengaluru Route Tollgate and other such toll gates, s hould be given priority. 
The Committee feels that this would allow smooth passage of city traffic as well as slow 
speed vehicles and lower the number of road accidents happening on the National 
Highways. 
(Para 42) 
Reply of the Ministry 
5.1     The service roads are provided only at urban/ semi -urban locations on NHs where 
local traffic is substantial and as such service roads are provided on a small length of 
NHs. 
5.2   However, as per the extant policy, for NH stretches developed to 6 -lane NH 
standards, th e service roads are provided in continuous length on both sides; unless 
otherwise specified for a project, the continuity is broken at locations of major bridges, 
at locations of toll plazas in a length of one km, in areas where no cross traffic or access 
traffic is expected provided the length of such section is at least one km. However, 
service roads may not be provided where there is no settlement or road side 
development abutting the Project Highway or the connecting roads are spaced more than 
2 km. 

4 
 
5.3   Service Road in a length of 40.838 Km has already been provided on NH -44 in 
Thondupally to Kurnool city section. Further, NHAI has also invited bids for 
construction of service road on both side from km.204.800 to 205.800 in Kurnool city 
for ensuring sa fety to local road users.  
 
MAINTENANCE AND REPAIR OF NATIONAL HIGHWAYS 
Recommendation/Observation 
6.   The Committee strongly rec ommends that  a mechanism should be es tablished to 
periodically monitor the quality of Highways. A policy fra mework should be set in place 
to ensure that  repair works and maintenan ce of Highways are carried out within  a 
prescribed tim eframe so  as to ens ure certain minimum  standards of pliability on t he 
Highways. 
(Para 46) 
Reply of the Ministry 
6.1    Regional Officers of the Ministry in consultation with concerned State PWDs 
continuously monitor the condition of National Highways and works on National 
Highways requiring maintenance and repair are taken up for execution as and when 
required to keep the highways in traffic worthy condition.  
6.2      Ministry has issued a guideline making the uses of Network Survey Vehicles 
(NSVs) mandatory. These vehicle s, besides collecting data related to road inventory will 
also help in capturing relevant data related  to the quality and serviceability condition of 
the NHs. 
6.3    A mechanism to measure the health condition of roads has been developed & the 
provisions of equipment -based monitoring, using NSVs, Falling Weight Deflectometer 
(FWD), Mobile Bridge Inspection  Unit (MBIU) etc. at specified intervals, have been 
incorporated in the consultancy agreements for all projects under implementation and 
Operations & Maintenance.   
6.4    Policy decisions were taken in August, 2018 to increase the concurrent defects 
liability cum maintenance periods for projects implemented on EPC mode to 5 years & 
10 years for flexible (bituminous) pavements and rigid (cement concrete) pavements 
respectively. Thus, EPC contractor is made responsible for concurrent maintenance and 
rectification of defects during the above -mentioned enhanced periods of 5/ 10 years as 
are relevant. This is expected to make Maintenance & Repair (M&R) of NHs more 
systematic and organized.  
6.5    As already mentioned, the Ministry has recently taken policy decisi on to allow 
booking / reimbursement of expenditures for ordinary / petty repairs carried out in a 
Financial Year (FY) as a spill over commitment on subsequent FY. This is expected to 
improve efficiency of booking of expenditure.  
6.6    The concerns of the Committee have been noted and the Ministry shall take all 
necessary actions towards ensuring proper M&R of NHs and better pliability of NHs.  
 
EXPRESSWAYS AND ECONOMIC CORRIDORS 

5 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
7.  The Committee notes that despite second largest road network in the w orld, India still 
lags behind in terms of length of Expressways. The Committee feels that Expressways are 
a crucial infrastructure requirement to ensure fast and seamless connectivity between the 
economic hubs of the country, as a l arge amount of  cargo and pa ssengers across  the 
country trav el by road. The Committee recommends the Ministry to work  out plans for  
more E xpressways in the country. Special attention be given to road quali ty and safety 
standards on Expressways since the vehicles travel at a fast speed and with low reaction 
time available to the drivers, wherein even the slightest fault in the road geometrics could 
lead to fatal accidents. 
(Para 60) 
Reply of the Ministry 
7.1     As a part of Bharatmala, 2,626 km of Expressways have been planned out of 
which 288 km were completed/UI before approval of Bharatmala Pariyojana. Out of the 
remaining 2,338 km, 659 km has already been awarded till 30th April 2020. Out of the 
remaining 1,6 79 km balance for award length, 1531 km will be targeted for award in the 
current Financial Year.

Delhi-Mumbai Expressway 
Recommendation/Observation 
8. The Committee would like to  know the present status of land acquisition and 
environmental/forest clearances for the 1351 km Delhi-Mumbai Expressway. The 
Committee feels that this is a vital project for improving the road connectivity between the 
two economic hotspots of the country and hopes that all efforts are made to ensure the 
timely completion of this  project. The Committee further recommends that given the 
immense length and potential of Delhi-Mumbai Expressway, mechanisms may be put in 
place to ensure that quality standards are maintained throughout the entire stretch of the 
Delhi-Mumbai Expressway. 
(Para 63) 
Reply of the Ministry 
8.1     The status of construction of Delhi-Mumbai Expressway is given at Annexure -I. 
8.2     Delhi-Mumbai Expressway from Delhi (Sohna) to Mumbai (Virar) is targeted for 
award in current FY 20 -21 with target for completion by January, 2023. Monitoring of 
the quality of construction of project expressway is being ensure d with routine and 
periodic testing of the quality of work done by the Contractor/Concessionaire.  
8.3    14,800 Ha of land needs to be acquired for the corridor. The land acquisition of the 
corridor is in advanced stage with 3D completed for 92% and 3G completed for 80% of 
land acquired. 
8.4    Status of Forest and Wildlife clearance is given at Annexure -II. 
 
FUNDING OF ROAD SECTOR PROJECTS 
Recommendation/Observation 

7 
 
9.  The Co mmittee appreciates the approval of the  proposed amendments to the  TOT 
model allowing operational NH projects with toll  revenue generation history of one year 
to be monetized through the TOT model and hopes that the same would enable the Ministry 
to raise more funds for its projects. The Committee desires that monitoring mechanisms 
should be put in  place to ensure that the O &M obligations which  rest with the  
concessionaires for such projects, are carried out with due earnest. 
(Para 67) 
Reply of the Ministry 
9.1     Field offices of NHAI ensure that O&M obligations of the Concessionaires for such 
projects are carried out with due earnest.. 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
10.  The Committee recommends that the Mini stry should look into the apprehensions of 
the conce ssionaires with reg ard to the  TOT mod el so as  to make  the TOT bundles 
attractive for more private players and thus generate higher funds.  
(Para 68) 
Reply of the Ministry 
10.1     The recommendations of the Committee is noted for further necessary action.  
 
WORKS UNDER ROADS WING 
Recommendation/Observation 
11.  The Committee notes a pattern of severe under-utilization of funds under the 
scheme„ EAP and Counterpart funding” during  the years 201 8-19 and 2019-20. The 
Committee would like to be app rised of the reaso ns behind this  underutilization. The 
Committee recommends that the Ministry may co ordinate with the St ate Governments 
involved, if any, to ensure optimal utilization under this head. 
(Para 93) 
Reply of the Ministry 
11.1   National Highways Interconnectivity Improvement Programme (NHIIP) under 
World Bank Loan Assistance –  
 8 projects out of 15 have already been completed. 3 works are in 
advanced stage of completion. Remaining 4 works are in the State of 
Bihar which ar e delayed mainly due to land acquisition and slow 
progress of the contractors. 3 out of 4 contractors are under the 
purview of NCLT and facing financial constraints. Now, on the 
request of the contractors, sub -contractors have been appointed to 
complete th e balance work. The projects are likely to be completed 
by June'2021.  
11.2    Regarding ADB funded projects, 2 projects under SASEC Tranche -I have been 
completed in 2019. In SASEC Tranche -II, the works got delayed due to LA issues as 

8 
 
these works are locat ed in North-Eastern states.  
11.3   JICA funded projects – 
 MoRTH project {NH -82 (Bihar Sharif -Rajgir-Gaya)} –Progress of 
the work is slow due to delay in land acquisition.  
 NHAI project {NH -83 (Patna -Gaya-Dobhi)} - Work is being 
implemented by NHAI. Due to financial constraints with the 
contractor M/s IL&FS Engineering Construction Company, the 
progress of the work was very slow. Due to this, it was decided to 
foreclose the project. For early completion of balance work, the 
stretch has been divided into thre e packages. Bids for Package -I 
(39km) was annulled & invited afresh; bids were received on 
01.07.2020 and are under evaluation. LOAs were issued for Item 
Rate contracts on 21.07.2020 for Packages -II (44km) & III (44.22km) 
for Rs. 496.48 Cr. & Rs. 464.10 Cr . respectively. These packages are 
likely to be completed by October, 2023.  
 NHIDCL projects {JICA Phase -I, II, III, IV} – These projects fall in 
the North-Eastern States of Meghalaya, Mizoram, Assam and Tripura 
where land acquisition has always been a maj or issue. NHIDCL is 
pursuing very hard with the concerned State Governments to expedite 
the land acquisition process so as to complete the work at the earliest.  
 
Recommendation/Observation 
12.    The Committee appreciates that 91.38% of the total allocation has been spent by the 
Ministry under NH(O) till January, 2020. The Committee, however, notes that there has 
been a slight reduction under  NH(O) in BE 2020-21 as compared to RE  2019-20, even 
when the Ministry has been able to spend almost the entire amount allocated for this 
head in 2019-20. The  Committee recommends that the Ministry of Road Transport and 
Highways should request the Ministry of Finance for higher allocation under this head at 
the RE 2020-21 stage. 
(Para 96) 
Reply of the Ministry 
12.1     The Ministry shall appropriately project additional funds requirements under RE 
2020-21. 
 
ACQUISITION OF LAND 
Recommendation/Observation 

9 
 
13.  The Committee takes note of the various initiatives taken by the Ministry to streamline 
the land acquisition process. While the introduction of Bhoomi Rashi Portal and the other

30.  The Committee recommends that the Ministry may install Electronic Weighing Bridges 
at Toll Booths in order to put a curb on rampant overloading of trucks in the country. The 
Committee feels that doing so would p revent damage to the roads and bridges, besides 
improving road safety. The Committee recommends that the Ministry may explore whether 
the Electronic Weighing system can be tied up with the Ele ctronic Toll Collection system

be overloaded, a challan is generated then and there for the vehicle. 
(Para 233) 
Reply of the Ministry 
30.1    NHAI has already issued directions to ROs to install Weigh in Motion in each 
lane. As on date, Weigh in Motion is installed in 377 plazas out of 613 fee plazas. For 
new projects / toll plaza medium speed WIM infrastructure are implemented in 
execution stage only.  
30.2    In existing system when Electronic Toll Collection (ETC) System is integrated 
with Weigh -in-Motion, it reads/identifies the FASTag affixed on the vehicle and deduct 
the fee applicable for that class of vehicle as per normal defined process (i.e., through 
Acquirer bank, NPCI and Issuer bank). If the vehicle is overloaded, applicable challan 
amount proportionate to the over -loading weight can be determined through the Weigh -
in-Motion system at the lane level or Static Weigh Bridge system near the plaza vicinity 
and can be handed over to the vehicle user. Thereafter, the exce ss fee or the challan 
amount can be paid in cash or other modes of payments at the fee plaza or collected 
through any other mechanism as provisioned.  
30.3    However, considering the fact that the penalty/challan amount is usually much 
more than the appli cable fee therefore it is proposed that same may not be deducted 
from FASTag account as there are possibilities that the FASTag may be pushed to 
negative/low balance and the vehicle may face issue while crossing the next fee plaza 
due to insufficient balan ce in the FASTag, if not recharged instantly. This may further 
increase number of blacklisted FASTags.

ROAD SAFETY 
Recommendation/Observation 
27.  The Committee notes that while the tot al number of road accidents has been 
decreasing since 2015, the number  of fatal road accidents is increa sing every year. The 
Committee would like the Ministry to evolve monitoring mechanisms for adherence of road 
safety standards at each stage of road construction and maintenance. 
(Para 188) 
Reply of the Ministry 
27.1     The following necessary safety measures are taken for the projects coming under 
the jurisdiction of NHAI: - 
 Provision of Safety Consultant/ Road Safety Expert is made in the 
projects by NHAI for proper monitoring with respect to Road Safety 
issues. 
 Also Training sessions are conducted for NHAI officials & 
IE/AE/Supervision Consultant in order to facilitate them for proper 
monitoring of Road Safety Standards. 
 Road Safety Audit is being conducted by NHAI before, during and post 
construction for adherence to road safety standards.  
 The Road Safety Audit recommendations submitted by Safety 
Consultants are communicated to concerned concessionaires/ contr actors 
for ensuring the implementation of these recommendations. 
 Each blackspot location is being inspected by Officers of Regional 
Offices, State PWDs/ RCDs (for stretches entrusted with State 
Governments), Project Director of Concerned PIU and Road Safet y 
Expert of the Independent Engineers (IE)/ Authority’s Engineers (AE) 
/Safety Consultants and recommend the mitigation measures.   
 Motor Vehicles (Amendment) Act, 2019 has been enforced since 
01.09.2019; these have new provisions as (1A) of section 116, ( 1A) of 
Section 138 etc., regarding Road Safety. 

36 
 
 Safety measures are being taken during construction by the respective 
concessionaire as per IRC guidelines and CA provisions and as per the 
suggestions/recommendations of safety expert of I.E or Safety Consul tant 
engaged for the respective project stretches. 
 Safe crossing facilities such as construction of VUP’s, PUP’s, FOB’s, 
service road, etc. are also being considered wherever required under 
safety reasons for the stretches under NHAI, based on recommendati ons 
of the standing committee consisting of Project Director, RSE of 
Independent Engineer, concerned local police authority and RSO of the 
RO, under delegation powers of RO vide circular No.1.1.27 dated 
20.03.2018. 
 Further, road safety week is conducted ev ery year to create safety 
awareness among the road users and also in various schools, villages/local 
public, and eye check -up camps for drivers etc., to reduce and prevent 
accidents.  
 For completed projects, Incident Management team is deployed at Toll 
Plazas on Highways consisting of Ambulances, Route Patrol Vehicles and 
Tow away cranes to provide medical help to victims as quickly as 
possible. 
 Paramedic with required equipment are mobilized for ambulance as per 
IRC guidelines/NHAI Extant Policy Circular issued from time to time. 
 The mobile app “Sukhad Yatra” has been developed which is used to 
provide the information related to Toll Plaza through GPS location and 
also implemented NHAI’s 24 X 7 Toll Free helpline number – 1033 for 
any incidence/emergency on  National Highways. Further, display boards 
(installed retro reflectorized sign boards) in this regard as per IRC codal 
provisions has been fixed on National Highways. Ambulances are 
equipped with Automatic vehicle tracking system with GPS technology 
for tracking vehicle’s current location. 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
28.  The Committee feels that one of the major reasons behind road accidents is the poor 
condition of roads. Presence of potholes can prove to be fatal, even more so in the rainy 
season. The  Committee re commends that the Mini stry may make provisions for  speedy 
redressal of s afety concerns on  National Hi ghways. The Committee fe els that  given the 
vast stretches of National Highways in the country, allowing road users to report potholes, 
lack of lighting, and other safety concerns through the use of smartphone application 
would be very helpful to rec eive info rmation on  such issues, along with pin point 
location. The Ministry/NHAI m ay then fo rward the  complaints received to the  
concessionaire, responsible for the maintenance of the concerned road. User feedback may 
also be sought on resolution of the reported issue. The Com mittee desires that such 
solutions may be implemented and sufficient fund be provided for that purpose. 
(Para 189)

during construction period Concession/Contract Agreements provide the specific 
provisions for all maintenance activities that shall be carried out by the Concessionaire 
under their obligations.  e.g. Article 12.4 under Concession Agreement of  Hybrid

free condition…” The response time for potholes is 48 hours. The respo nse time for 
lighting defects is 24 hours for any major failure of the system while it is only 8 hours 
for faults and minor failures. The resources should be accordingly allocated for such top 
class protocol to have world class roads.  
28.2   Complaints re garding maintenance can be lodged by users on toll free no. 1033. 
Reporting of Potholes is already included in the “Sukhad Yatra” Mobile App.

ANNUAL PLAN 2019-20 
The Committee is concerned to note the pattern of low spending under several key 
Heads, especially Maintenance & Repair (M&R). The Committee observes that the 
projected requirement of the Ministry for M&R for  FY 2019 -20 was Rs. 6,500 
crores, but the Ministry could not utilize even the allocated amount of Rs. 2,000 
crores. The Committee urges the Ministry to avoid such ritualistic allocations which 
remain on paper only and recommends that the Ministry should ma ke all out efforts 
to ensure optimum fund utilization under all the major Heads, laying special focus 
on the Maintenance & Repair Head. 
(Para 1.10) 
 
The Committee notes that the Ministry has merely chosen to note its observations 
for compliance and no specific mention has been made or details furnished of the 
initiatives taken by the Ministry to resolve the issues that are presently preventing 
the Ministry from ensuring optimum utilization of funds. The Committee, therefore, 
urges upon the Ministry to t ake concrete steps to ensure balanced expenditure of 
funds allocated to the Ministry in all the quarters of a Financial Year.  
(Para 2.2) 
 
The Committee terms the reasons furnished by the Ministry as routine in nature. 
The Ministry has been casual in its a pproach while launching these projects without 
making any assessment as to actual fund requirements and the corpus of fund seems 
to have been arbitrarily decided without reference to ground realities. The 
Committee would like the Ministry to be proactive w hile tackling the issues causing 
slow pace of expenditure, since delays in infrastructure projects cause significant 
cost overruns over period of time.  
(Para 4.3) 
 
The Committee is not convinced by the reasons furnished by the Ministry for under -
utilization of funds for Maintenance & Repair, Research & Development and Road 
Transport Heads. The Committee opines that instead of surrendering funds 
allocated to M&R for enhancing matching allocation to NH(O) Head, the Ministry 

83 
 
should have examined the reasons t hat led to low expenditure under this Head and 
strived to resolve them. The Committee observes that the funds are released to the 
States under M&R and R&D schemes on the basis of fulfillment of certain 
conditionalities by the State Governments/ implementin g agencies, such as 
submission of Utilization Certificates and Audited Statements, regularization of 
expenditures, completion of pre-construction activities, etc. Some of the States could 
not fulfill the conditions prescribed. The Committee is constrained to note that apart 
from administrative failure of the recipient States in fulfilling the conditions, the 
Ministry is also not in a position to estimate the extent of utilization of allotted sums 
and examine the feasibility of attaining the mandatory condit ions by the States. 
Taking the above into consideration, the Committee would like the Ministry to 
review the conditions and make them more flexible in order to enable the States to 
fully utilize the Grants. The Committee would also recommend to the Ministr y to 
enter into Memorandum of Understanding with the recipient States so as to act in a 
coordinated manner to overcome the shortcomings in utilization of budgeted funds.

Committee, against delays caused on part of the concessionaires.  
(Para 21.3) 
 
The Committee is of the view that such long delays cannot be tolerated in strategic 
areas such as the North -East. The Committee, therefore, recommends that a 
dedicated mechanism be put in place to look into and resolve the factors causing 
delays in complet ion of the SARDP -NE Phase -A as well as future Central road 
projects in the North-East.  
(Para 22.3) 
 
The Committee reiterates its recommendation made in Para 22.3 in Chapter III of 
this Report.  

87 
 
(Para 23.3) 
 
CHARDHAM PARIYOJANA 
The Committee takes note of the reasons that have led to the delay in the timely 
completion of the Chardham Pariyojana. The Committee feels that this Chardham 
project is of great significance to bolster domestic as well as foreign tourist influx in 
the regions it connects. The Commit tee, therefore, recommends that the Ministry 
may communicate with the MoEF&CC / HPC requesting them to expedite the final 
report in this matter so as to minimize further delays on this important project.  
(Para 24.5) 
 
BHARATMALA PARIYOJANA PHASE-I 
The Comm ittee notes that the Ministry has not furnished the reasons behind the 
delays in Bharatmala Pariyojana Phase -I, which is a flagship project to serve the 
infrastructural requirements of the country. The Committee recommends that the 
Ministry assess in detai l, the reasons behind the delays and its impact on the 
budgetary requirements for this Phase. The Ministry may then develop a revised 
timeline, work out the revised budgetary requirements for completion of rest of the 
BM Phase-I and make sincere efforts to abide by the same.  
(Para 25.3) 
 
PROJECTS LINKED TO COASTAL ROADS AND PORT CONNECTIVITY 
The Committee is distressed to note that less than 10% of the 2000 km length of 
coastal and port connectivity roads identified for development under Bharatmala 
Phase-I, has been awarded till now, even when the targeted completion for 
Bharatmala Phase -I is 2021 -22. The Committee desires that the Ministry may 
urgently look into the reasons behind this inordinate delay. The timely completion of 
the 2000 km length of  coastal and port connectivity roads identified for BM Phase -I 
is directly linked with the performance of the Shipping sector of the country and 
thus, all efforts must be made by the Ministry to resolve the bottlenecks causing 
delay in this project.  
(Para 26.4) 
 
ECONOMIC CORRIDORS AND STRATEGIC HIGHWAYS 
The Committee notes the progress made by NHAI and NHIDCL in this regard. The 
Committee is of the view that a large portion of the length targeted under 
Bharatmala Pariyojana Phase-I has not even been awarde d yet, and thus, it is likely 
to miss the completion target set for 2021 -22. The strategic importance of Border 

88 
 
and International connectivity roads cannot be overstated. The Committee 
recommends that the Ministry should make all necessary efforts to keep the 
completion of development of the Border and International connectivity roads on 
track.  
(Para 27.2) 
 
DELAYS IN ROAD PROJECTS 
The Committee takes note of the various efforts being made by the Ministry to 
minimize delays in its road projects. However, it  is clear from the major delays 
noticed in majority of road projects that the efforts of the Ministry are not yielding 
the required results. Delays in road projects not only cause significant inconvenience 
to the road users but create avoidable stress on t he financial health of the Ministry, 
as well as the sectors dependent on road connectivity in a particular region. In light 
of this, the Committee reiterates the recommendation made in Para 178 of its 278 th 
Report on Demands for Grants (2020 -21) of Ministr y of Road Transport and 
Highways seeking establishment of a Special Delay Mitigation Cell dedicated to 
address delays in ongoing road projects of the Ministry.  
(Para 28.9) 
 
Noting that no action seems to have been taken on creation of a dedicated body wit h 
the sole objective of minimizing and mitigating delays in the various projects of the 
Ministry, the Committee reiterates the recommendation made in Para 28.9 in 
Chapter III of this Report.  
(Para 29.2) 
 
CO-ORDINATION WITH STATE GOVERNMENTS 
The Committee appreciates that the existing schemes are being implemented by the 
Ministry in co -ordination with State Governments to bolster their public transport 
system. The Committee further desires that the Ministry may work out a scheme to 
provide special financial  as well as technical support, wherever possible, to public 
transportation systems for the States which tackle issues related to high pollution 
every year.  
(Para 30.4) 
 
STAFFING IN NHAI 
The Committee notes with concern that NHAI is still grappling with large number of 
vacant posts. For overcoming the problem, NHAI has initiated certain measures 
which include revision of Recruitment Rules, filling vacancies on direct and 

89 
 
deputation basis, etc. The Committee apprehends that these measures might not be 
enough to tide over the issue of shortage of manpower in the short term. The 
Committee would therefore recommend that NHAI may explore the avenue of 
engaging skilled manpower on contract basis to address the problem of shortage of 
skilled manpower.  
(Para 31.4) 
 
MISCELLANEOUS 
CAG Report on Hyderabad-Bengaluru Toll Road 
The Committee desires to know the course of action being planned by NHAI in the 
light of the balance in the Escrow Account being insufficient for recovery of the 
damages. The Committee may also be apprised of the action taken by the Ministry / 
NHAI to ensure that such cases do not recur in the future.  
(Para 32.2) 
 
Public Project Monitoring Facility 
The Committee appreciates the initiative taken by NHAI for publication of 
information about its projects on its website ( https://nhai.gov.in/project-website.htm). 
The Committee, however, notes that several key columns are yet to be updated in 
respect of the projects displayed on this webpage. The Committee, therefore, 
recommends that information regarding concessionaires working on the projects 
and details of officer(s) responsible for ensuring desired quality for a particular 
project, may also be published on the project details page.  
(Para 33.5) 
 
Promotion of Electric Vehicles in the country 
The Committee is of the view that electric vehicles are going to be ubiquitous in the 
near future, given their economic as well as environmental benefits. The Committee 
would like to know the reasons for deferring the proposal for exemption of 
registration fees for battery operated/ electric vehicles. The Committee feels that 
exempting registration fees for electric vehicles will give a boost to the demand for 
such vehicles in the country. The Ministry of Road Transport and Highways, in close 
co-ordination with other Ministries concerned, should strive for setting up the 
necessary infrastructure for this inevitable transition. The demand thus created, will 
also push domestic vehicle manufacturers to start giving more importance to this up 
and coming segment.  The Committee notes that countries like Norway, besides 
granting exemption from vehicle acquisition tax and several other incentives, even 
went to the extent of exempting electric vehicles from toll taxes. As a result of such 
incentives, more than 50% of new car sales in Norway are now electric vehicles. The 

90 
 
Committee recommends that the Ministry may examine the electric vehicles policies 
being adopted worldwide as well as Delhi Electric Vehicles Policy, 2020 and come 
out with a lucrative electric vehicle policy with a view to promote/ incentivize the 
adoption of electric vehicles in the country.  
(Para 34.2) 
 
Coordination with Local Police Departments 
The Committee notes the reply. The Committee, however, feels that the above 
mentioned policy of the Minist ry to not permit erection of check barriers on 
National Highways except in certain situations mentioned in their reply, is not 
actually implemented on ground since vehicles being stopped for checking of 
documents is a common sight, even on National Highway s. The Committee, 
therefore, recommends that the Ministry may write to all the State Governments to 
intimate/ remind them about the relevant policy in this regard.  
(Para 35.3) 
 

91

OF THE MINISTRY IS STILL AWAITED

CHAPTER I 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS WHICH HAVE BEEN ACCEPTED BY THE 
MINISTRY 
Jawaharlal Nehru Port 
PORT PERFORMANCE 
Recommendation/Observation  
1. The Committee notes the increased efficiency of the Port in terms of containers handled 
at 0.43% and the increase in average output per ship Berth day overall at 1.50% over the 
previous years.  The Committee commends the ef ficient management of the Port authorities in  
improving the efficiency parameters of the Port in order to make it as competitive as some of the 
best ports in the world.                           (Para 64)              
2. The Committee applauds the steps ta ken to improve the infrastructure facilities of JNPT 
and would urge upon the Government to further upgrade and modernize the Port to assure 
improved performance benchmarking against global standards.           (Para 67) 
Reply of the Ministry 
2.1 The improv ement in the performance has continued in the year 2018 -19 also. During 
Apr.-Dec., 2018, the total traffic handled at port was up by 7.39% as compared to same period of 
last year. The Output Per Shipberth day was also up by 3.7%. The vessel pre -berthing detention 
and turnaround time have come down by 18.5% & 5.75% respectively.  
2.2 The Port has undertaken series of projects to enhance the capacity and upgrade facilities 
to ensure improved performance. The project under implementation stage includes:  
 Construction of Coastal Berth: Dedica ted facility for coastal cargo out of custom bound area 
with separate approach road.   
 Capital Dredging work: To facilitate berthing of larger container vessels with deeper draft.   
 Construction of SEZ: To provide impetus for development of port based industry. 

3 
 
 Parking Plaza: The facility for direct entry of factory stuffed containers with in Customs 
Processing Zone.  
 Dry Ports at Jalna & Wardha: To connect hinterland directly with Port. 
 Widening of roads:  widening of Port roads connecting national highways. 
Vishakhapatnam Port Trust 
PROFITABILITY 
Recommendation/Observation  
3. The Committee takes note of the profit after tax to the tune of Rs. 189.46 crores. 
However, in order to assess the operational efficiency of the Port a nd its competitiveness 
as also to suggest measures to improve its productivity, the Committee desires to be kept 
apprised of the Return on Capital Employed (ROCE) for the Port.         (Para 98) 
Reply of the Ministry 
3.1. It may be noted that the profit after tax is to the tune of Rs.195.87 crores and VPT 
has registered 19.69% return on Capital employed during 2017-18. 
VOC Port Trust 
TRAFFIC 
Recommendation/Observation 
4. Moreover, the Committee feels that the proximity of P orts, both private and major, alon g 
the coast, cater to the same hinterland. The number of P orts is far larger than the demand for 
them. The supply exceeds the demand and this has resulted in the underutilization of the 
economies of scale. The Committee fails to understand the lack of plan ning and foresight in the 
operation of this port and the neglect of the Port by the Ministry of Shipping  and the State 
Government.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Ministry of Shipping must focus its 
attention on the development of the Port a s a transshipment hub. The Committee recommends 
that the Port must reduce its reliance on bulk cargo in terms of coal etc. and change its business 
model in order to attract more varied traffic.            (Para 124) 

4

4.1 VOCPT has tak en a number of steps to develop the Port as a Transshipment Hub given 
its proximity to East –West Sea Trade Route for which the following short term initiatives have 
been taken: 
 Increase in Permissible draft, LOA and Beam at Container Terminals upto 14.2m, 310m 
& 48m respectively. 
 67% Concession in Vessel Related Charges offered for mainline vessels. 
 Mv. Wan Hai, First Mainline vessel connecting Far East is calling VOCPT since 
12.12.18. 
4.2 As of December, 2017, VOC P ort was able to handle 12.8m draft vessel s inside the Port. 
Considering the increase in the traffic and to handle bigger size vessels the port has increased the 
draft from 12.8 to 14.2m at berths 8, 9, NCB I, CJ I and CJ II. Taking advantage of the P ort is 
now handling vessels upto 14.2m at berth no.9 and NCB I for handling of bulk cargoes. 
4.3 In respect of conversion of VOC P ort as transshipment hub MoS engaged consultants 
(AECOM) to study the traffic forecast and for development of infrastructure facilities. Now as 
per the suggestion of MoS , Port engaged NTCPWC, I .I.T. Chennai to prepare a master plan for 
strengthening of the berths and to propose new container terminal for handling of bigger size 
container vessels. 
4.4 As per this plan it is proposed to modernize the existing infrastructure and  to develop 
new container terminal in four phases from 2019 -20 to 2034 -35. In the master plan there is 
proposal for development of 2 container terminals for a quay length of more than 1000m at the 
outer harbour and dredging upto ( -) 15.5m in first phase ba sed on the traffic and size of the 
vessels. 
4.5 As an immediate step P ort has taken steps to convert the existing berth no. 9 into a 
container berth and subsequently the berths VOC 1,2,3,4 will be converted into container berths.

Chennai Port Trust 
POLICY INITIATIVES 
Recommendation/Observation 
6. Chennai Port, given its location, is suitable for the purposes of tourism as it has been a 
gateway to the South.  The Committee further recommends that the Port should follow the 
example of the Mumbai Port Trust a nd re -design and develop cruise terminals for                
tourists/passengers.                (Para 148)

6.1 A State of Art Cruise Passenger Facilitation Centre with all mandatory clearance viz.,

Cochin Port Trust

CRUISE TERMINAL 
Recommendation/Observation  
7. The Committee is pleased to note the steps taken by the Port in developing a 
passenger cruise terminal. This is a neglected aspect of shipping in India and is a major 
source of revenue in other nations. Cruise Tourism must be pursued with greater vigor 
and the Committee is pleased to know that the Ministry of Tourism is cooperating with 
the Ministry of Shipping to develop Cruise Terminals.             (Para 171 A) 
Reply of the Ministry 
  7.1. Cochin Port is one of the most preferred cruise destinations on the western coast of 
India and figures on the itinerary of most of the cruise lines that visit the Indian coast. 
Cochin Port has pioneered several initiatives to promote cruise shipping and to position 
itself as a preferred port of call. 
  7.2. Cochin Port handles cruise ships complying with the Standard Operating 
Procedure (SOP) issued by the Ministry of Tourism . Cochin Port has already in place a 
full air conditioned cruise terminal measuring 1800 sq.m area with dedicated counters for 
Customs and Immigration, scanner etc. In ad dition to this, in order to cope  up with the 
potentials of the growth in the cruise business, a new cruise terminal with 2253 sq.m area 
with all facilities has been constructed at a cost of Rs.25.72 Cr funded by the M inistry of 
Tourism. In 2018 -19, CoPT handled 49 cruise ships and in 2019 -20, 44 ships were 
facilitated.   
7.3. Major steps taken by the Cochin Port in developing a passenger cruise terminal 
are: 
1)       Introduction of rationalized tariff for cruise ships 
2) New initiatives like e -visa and e -landing card have been introduced by 
Immigration Department for the easy facilitation of cruise passengers. 
3) Substantial discounts in Vessel related charges are granted to cruise ships. 

8 
 
4) Spaces for Kiosks are allotted to promo te local trade offering souvenir, 
local cuisine, ethnic apparels, local artisan etc.  
5) ITDC operates duty free shops inside the Customs bonded area. 
6) Prepaid auto/taxi services operated by DTPC duly verifying the credentials 
of the drivers. 
7) Free WiFi to Cruise passengers is available at the terminal. 
8) Battery operated Buggies for passengers are also available. 
9) Sufficient Parking area for Tourist coaches. 
10) Helicopter service was operated on trial basis from the terminal to various 
tourist destinations of Kerala during the last financial year. 
7.4. Cochin Port recognizes cruise tourism as a potential area of growth and shall 
endeavor to take on board all the stakeholders to promote Cochin Port as a preferred 
cruise destination. 
Emerging Constellation of Container Terminals in South India 
Recommendation/Observation  
8. Investment in smaller new Ports in India can yield much better returns as they would 
service vessels on coastal and inland waterway. The Committee feels that the three ports coming 
up within a distanc e of about 130 nautical miles need to be developed and strategized in such a 
manner that all the three receive sufficient cargo to ensure profitable operations. The Committee 
thus recommends that infrastructure development of one port should not be at the cost of the 
development of another nearby port.             (Para 246) 
Reply of the Ministry 
8.1 Observations of the Committee have been noted. 
Recommendation/Observation  
9. The Committee recommends that efforts must be concentrated on the development and  
expansion of infrastructure that would make water transport more attractive, instead of 
prioritizing road transport and turn already over -crowded highways into death traps. More 

9 
 
emphasis must be placed on the coast route and inland waterways as a mode of transport for 
hinterland cargo connectivity and its development must be made a priority.       (Para 247) 
Reply of the Ministry 
9.1 Government declared 111 (including 5 existing and 106 new) National Waterways 
(NWs) spread over 24 states under the National  Waterways Act, 2016, which came into effect 
from 12 April, 2016 to promote Inland Water Transport (IWT) in the country.  
9.2 Out of these 111 waterways, NWs – 1, 2 and 3 are operational and cargo and passenger 
vessels are moving on them. The development works on NW-4 under Phase-I had commenced in 
2017 and pre-project activities have been initiated on NW-5.   
9.3 In addition, Government is implementing the Jal Marg Vikas Project (JMVP) at an 
estimated cost of Rs. 5369.18 crore for capacity augmentation of navigation on National 
Waterway-1 (NW -1) on the Haldia – Varanasi stretch of Ganga -Bhagirathi- Hooghly River 
System with the technical and financial assistance of the World Bank. The salient features of the 
project are construction of three multimodal term inals at Haldia (West Bengal), Sahibganj 
(Jharkhand), Varanasi (U.P.) and two intermodal terminals at Kalughat (Bihar), Ghazipur (U.P.); 
five pairs of Ro -Ro terminals at Rajmahal (Jharkhand) -Manikchak (West Bengal), Samdaghat 
(Jharkhand)-Manihari (Bihar), Kahalgaon-Tintangha (Bihar), Hasnapur -Bakhtiyarpur (Bihar),  
Buxer (Bihar)-Saraikota (U.P.); and  one new navigational lock at Farakka (West Bengal). JMVP 
is scheduled to be completed in March, 2023. 
9.4. Based on the outcome of techno -economic feasibility and Detailed Project Reports 
(DPRs) prepared for new 106 NWs, technical interventions are being planned for safe navigation 
and shipping on technically viable NWs. As per the DPRs completed so far for the new NWs, 36 
NWs have been found to be technically viable.  
Cargo Evacuation from Indian Ports in Terms of Transport Mode 
Recommendation/Observation  
10. Furthermore, the Committee recommends that evacuation of cargo to and from the port 
areas have to be properly synchronized so that the inter -modal network  functions smoothly. 
Road and rail connectivity form an integral part of the port infrastructure as inefficient 

10 
 
evacuation of cargo can undermine the entire operation of a port. In particular, containerization 
of cargo presupposes a seamless link with the road and rail network in an ‘end to end’ transport 
system. Congestion at ports results in delayed evacuation of cargo due to inadequate road and 
rail capacity. This adversely impacts the competitiveness of Indian industry. Port connectivity 
has ramifications that go beyond the operation of a port per se.          (Para 252) 
Reply of the Ministry 
10.1 Observations of the Committee have been noted. 
Cabotage Laws 
Recommendation/Observation  
11. The Committee recommends that a study must be conducted on the eff ects of Cabotage 
Laws in the shipping sector of the country. The Committee feels that research must be conducted 
as to why, given the reduction of the Cabotage laws, the Ports have witnessed a paltry level of 
transshipment. The policy of the Ministry in th is regard must be scientifically monitored and 
solutions to the same must be devised. The Committee extends its full cooperation in this matter 
as it feels that the success of transshipment hubs in the country is essential for the growth of 
Ports in India.                (Para 261) 
Reply of the Ministry 
11.1 Effects of relaxation of Cabotage laws are regularly being monitored particularly impact 
on transshipment. As per the recent trends (u pto December, 2018), the transshipment details are 
given as under: 
a.   The number of Indian EXIM containers handled in India has increased from 6.4 Million 
TEUs in April – December FY16 TO 7.9 Million TEUs in April – December FY19. 
b.  The overall container traffic in Indian ports has increased from 99 MMT in April – 
December FY16 to 126 MMT in April – December FY19 at a CAGR OF 8% in the backdrop of 
this, the growth of containers transshipped in Indian ports has increased by 33% CAGR in the 
same period indicating a significant increase in share of Indian ports in transshipment. 

11 
 
c.  The growth in container transshipment through Indian ports was 26% in tonnage terms 
and 25% in TEUs terms during April – December, 2018 against the corresponding period of last 
year. 
11.2 Overall, India aims to reduce transshipment of its contai ners at foreign ports such as 
Colombo, Singapore, Jebel Ali, etc, in order to reduce logistics costs for Indian traders and time 
and conserve valuable foreign exchange for the country, while simultaneously supporting 
economic growth and jobs in India that would otherwise be lost to other countries that handle 
Indian cargo during transshipment. 
11.3 Shipping lines do their route planning on an annual basis at the very least and changing 
schedule of services along with accompanying partners requires careful p lanning and operational 
management by them. It takes 2 to 3 years from commencement to firmly establish 
transshipment and hence the effect of recent cabotage relaxation by India coupled with an 
infrastructure push, rationalization of tariffs, procedure sim plification (such as inter -terminal 
transfer), etc, is expected to take some time to manifest.

Recommendation/Observation

14.1 Ministry of Shipping / IWAI has developed the following Ro-Ro terminals/ facilities in

Efficiency of the Port Sector Operations 
Recommendation/Observation  
15. The Committee feels that low productivity and high vessel turnaround t ime at Indian 
ports are due to: (i) Low level of mechanization and insufficient draft; (ii) Skewed handling 
capacity for different types of cargo; and (iii) Infrastructure constraints in hinterland 
connectivity. It has been observed that lagging behind oth er countries on performance 
parameters pushes up the cost of trade and renders Indian ports less competitive. Non -Major 
Ports have fared well, ensuring quicker turnaround by investing in the infrastructure to handle 
larger vessels. Considering the strategic location of India’s Major Ports and their importance to 
trade, there is an opportunity to improve their performance to meet global benchmarks. Most of 
the Major Ports have high Turnaround Time  even while the utilization level is low and only a 
few have the ability to handle bigger cape -size vessels. The shipping industry is moving towards 
cape-size vessels. So, it is important that India develops cape handling capability at its key ports 
to ensure economics of scale for the trade.             (Para 231) 
Reply of the Ministry 
15.1 While increasing the capacity of major ports, Ministry of Shipping  has been striving to 
improve the operational efficiencies through mechanization, digitization and process 
simplification. The Average Turnaround Time during 2018 -19 improved to 59.85 Hrs from 
96.00 Hrs during 2014 -15. The Average Output Per Ship Berthday has increased from 12458 
Tonnes in 2014-15 to about 16434 Tonnes during 2018-19.   
15.2 Ministry of Shipping had identified various parameters under Ease of Doing B usiness for 
reducing dwell time and transaction costs in the Major Ports. These include elimination of 
manual forms, accommodation for laboratories to Participating Government Agencies (PGAs), 
Direct Port Delivery, Installation of Container Sca nners, e -delivery orders, RFID based g ate-
automation System, etc. These initiatives have already been implemented at Jawaharlal Nehru 
Port Trust (JNPT) and are being taken up in other Major Ports. 
15.3 Lack of draft in some of the Major Ports has been an area of concern, which is hampering 
handling of larger vessels and consequently affecting the growth in cargo traffic. A great focus is 
being given on the issue of enhancing the draf t of ports. 10 of the 12 Major P orts have already 

31 
 
achieved a draft of 14 mtrs or above.  Steps are being taken to further increase the draft in the 
Major Ports so that they are able to handle larger vessels and are in a position to compete wi th

Major Issues Ailing Cargo Management in The Major Ports 
Draft Limitations 
Recommendation/Observation  
26. The Committee has observed that the relatively low draft at Indian P orts do not measure 
upto internationally set standards. Presently, vesse ls greater than 11,000 TEU are in service. 
The movement towards larger ships is driven by economics of scale. It follows that in case of 
containership for 1,000 TEU capacities, the average draft is 8.3 meter, which increases to 15.5 
metres for ships above 11,000 TEU capacities. Container vessels with a capacity of 4,000 TEU 
require a minimum draft of 12.5 meters.            (Para 223) 
27. The Committee feels that there is a need to maximize the utilization of these vessels, 
which will in turn lead to reduct ion in the number of port calls on major routes and push for the 
development of global mega ports served by fully integrated global network. Most Major Ports 

57 
 
in India have minimum draft under 12m, except for a few of the younger ports which have draft 
of more than 14m. Insufficient draft at Indian Ports leads to increased costs and time taken as 
cargo originating fro m and those that are bound for I ndia gets routed through tr ansshipment 
ports like Colombo and Singapore. The Committee feels that as vessels ke ep getting bigger, 
Indian ports need deeper drafts, which call for increased and greater investments in capital 
dredging.                 (Para 224) 
Reply of the Ministry 
27.1 Major capital dredging projects are proposed to be undertaken for increasing dra fts in 
Major Ports. In most of the Major Ports, 14 meters draft has been achieved except Kolkata Port 
where it is not feasible. Mormugao Port and Kamarajar Port Ltd. are b eing dredged to handle 18 
meter draft vessels, which are largest available  globally. At present, 18 meter d raft is available 
only in outer harbour of Visakhapatnam Port. 
Further recommendation/observation: 
27.2 The Committee is aware that drafts at Indian Ports have historically been low both 
in the channel and at berths. The Committee not es from the reply of the Ministry  that 14  
meter draft has been achieved in most of the Major Ports . C onsidering the fact that top 
container Ports in the world have achieved draft depth ranging from 14 m to 16 m long 
back and some Ports have enhanced this still further, there is a  need that draft for our 
Major Ports should be beyond 14 m in order to cater to the requirement of new generation 
ships. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Ministry of Shipping should ensure 
that the Major Ports underta ke the dredging work to increase their draft dep th to 18 
meters within a definite  timeline. Since the dredging is highly capital intensive, the 
Committee would like to know as to how the Major Ports would meet their expenditure 
towards the capital and main tenance dredging and whether the dredging, if funded 
through internal resources and borrowings would entail the increase in their overall Port 
cost and consequently tariff.   
27.3 The Ministry should also provide reasons for the non -feasibility in implemen tation 
of major capital dredging p rojects at Kolkata Port. T he Committee would also like  the 

58 
 
Ministry to provide port-wise details alongwith the status of implementation of the projects

Role of Tariff Regulations at India’s Major Ports 
Recommendation/Observation  
28. The Committee feels that the Port sector in India is facing certain tariff - related 
uncertainties due to multiplicity of regimes. The non -Major Ports do not come under any tariff 
jurisdiction and price their services based on market and competition. But the major ones 
(including private terminals therein) fall under the jurisdiction of a regulator viz, Tariff 
Authority for Major Ports (TAMP). This anomaly and the lack of a level playin g field have long 
been debated issue.                  (Para 227) 
Reply of the Ministry 
28.1 The Major Port Trusts and the BOT Terminals operating there were initially covered by 
the Tariff Guidelines of 2005. The Tariff Guidelines of 2005 did not provide flexibility to the 
Port Trusts and the BOT Terminals in pricing of their services. The Port Trusts and the BOT 
Terminals operating there have been taken out of the Tariff Guidelines of 2005 and now are 
covered under the Tariff Policy, 2018 (Major Port Trus ts) and the Tariff Guidelines, 2019 (BOT 
Terminals), which give them flexibility to price their services within their Annual Revenue 
Requirement. 
Further recommendation/observation: 
28.2 The Committee notes the reply. The Committee, however, desires to kno w whether 
tariff has been left entirely to the market forces or a norm based tariff is fixed by the 
regulator. 
Recommendation/Observation  
29. In view of the considerable loss of business opportunities for the Major Ports due to the 
provision of certain ta riff related uncertainties as ascertained by TAMP, the Committee 
recommends that the anomalies in the TAMP rules must be made reasonable in order to make it 
lucrative for ships to call on Major Ports against private ports. The Committee further 

59 
 
recommends that the role of the TAMP must be redefined and that a strategic and market 
oriented system of tariff must be set in place.                       (Para 229) 
Reply of the Ministry 
29.1 The Major Port Trusts and the BOT operating there were initially covered  by the Tariff 
Guidelines of 2005. The Tariff Guidelines of 2005 did not provide flexibility to the Port Trusts 
and the BOT Terminals in pricing of their services. The Port Trusts and the BOT Terminals 
operating threat have been taken out of the Tariff Gui delines of 2005 and now are covered under 
the Tariff Policy, 2018 (Major Port Trusts) and the Tariff Guidelines, 2019 (BOT Terminals), 
which give them flexibility to price their services within their Annual Revenue Requirement. 
29.2 Regarding redefining ro le of TAMP it is stated that steps have already been initiated by 
the Government in this direction. A Major Port Authorities Bill, 2016 was introduced in the Lok 
Sabha in December, 2016, inter -alia, envisaging setting up an Adjudicatory Board, which will 
carry out other than tariff setting functions of TAMP and will adjudicate and look into any 
disputes, claims arising between Major Ports, BOT operators to revive stressed projects. 
29.3 The Committee has also recommended that a strategic and market oriented  system of 
tariff must be set in place. In this regard, it is stated that the Traffic Policy, 2018 of Major Port 
Trusts and Tariff Guidelines of 2019 for BOT Terminals which were earlier governed by 2005 
Tariff Guidelines provide for market oriented system  of tariff fixation which will make it 
lucrative for more ships to call on Major Ports. 
Further recommendation/observation: 
29.4 The Committee observes that the Major Port Authorities Bill was introduced in the 
Lok Sabha in December 2016 but no further progress has been reported since then, which 
is indicative of the Ministry’s inertia in the matter. The Committee would expect the 
Ministry to take an early decision to thrash out all the lingering issues once for all and 
carry out a comprehensive review of the various provisions of the aforesaid Bill, so that the 
necessary changes which are in tune with the present needs are accommodated and those 
provisions which are no longer required, are eliminated. The Committee desires to be kept 
apprised of the action taken in this regard.

REPORT 
INTRODUCTION 
    Road Transport plays a critical role in the economic growth of any country. The 
necessity for the continued need for strengthening the road network in the country is 
underscored by the fact that the transport sector contributed abo ut 4.6 percent in the Gross 
Value Added (GVA) for F inancial Year 2018-19, of which the share of road transport was 
about 67 percent (Economic Survey 2020 -21, Volume -2). A robust, safe, well -maintained 
road network would be key for our country to overcome t he damaging impact of the 
Coronavirus pandemic on the national economy. 
2. The tasks and responsibilities of the Ministry of Road Transport and Highways 
encompass, inter alia , construction and maintenance of National Highways (NHs); 
administration of the Nati onal Highways Act,  1956; National Highways Authority of India 
Act, 1988; National Highways Fee (Determination of Rates and Collection) Rules, 2008; 
Motor Vehicles Act 1988; and Central Motor Vehicles Rules 1989, as also formulation of 
broad policies relating to road transport and automotive norms, besides making arrangements 
for movement of vehicular traffic with neighbouring countries. 
3. India has the second largest road network in the world of about 62.16 lakh km. This 
comprises National Highways, Expresswa ys, State Highways, Major District Roads, Other 
District Roads and Village Roads as under: 
National Highways 1,36,440 km 
State Highways 1,76,818 km 
Other Roads 59,02,539 km 
Total 62,15,797 km 
 
4. The associated offices under the Ministry of Road Transport  and Highways are as 
follows:  

2 
 
i. National Highways Authority of India (NHAI):   
Set up through an Act of Parliament in 1988, NHAI is responsible for the 
development, maintenance and management of the National Highways entrusted to it 
and for matters related or incidental there to. The NHAI became operational in 
February, 1995. 
ii. National Highways & Infrastructure Development Corporation Ltd. (NHIDCL) : 
NHIDCL is a corporate entity under the Ministry, responsible for the construction/ up-
grading/widening of Natio nal Highways in parts of the country which share 
international boundaries with neighbouring countries in order to promote regional 
connectivity on a sustainable basis. 
iii. Indian Academy of Highway Engineers (IAHE):  
The Indian Academy of Highway Engineers (IA HE) is a registered Society under the 
administrative control of the Ministry. It is a collaborative body which was set up in 
the year 1983 with the objective of fulfilling the long felt need for training of 
Highway Engineers in the country, both at the ent ry level and during their service 
period. 
iv. Indian Road Congress (IRC):  
The IRC was formally registered as a Society on 24 th September 1937 under the 
Societies Registration Act of 1860 for periodical holding of road conferences to 
discuss issues related to road construction, maintenance & development.

Quality Inspection 
60. Quality of the construction activities are being checked at site timely as per specifications 
of MoRTH by the Authority Engineer and by concerned Officers posted at Site and at the 
Regional Offices. Poor quality  work found (if any) is immediately rectified by the EPC 
contractor. NHAI has implemented a system for Quality inspection of NHAI projects 
during construction by engaging Retired Officials from State PWD, MoRTH, BRO etc. 
Suitable actions are also initiated  against defaulting Contractors/Consultants.In addition 
to that, a panel of Independent Special Project Monitors (SPMs) have been set up by 
NHIDCL and the SPMs have been engaged from time to time to check the quality of 
work at Site. 
61. A Quality Control Zone has also been created in the Ministry in September, 2020 headed 
by Chief Engineer with an objective that Quality Control Zone will work towards the 

24 
 
preparation of policy guidelines as well as examine and issue directions/suggestions for 
system improvement on Quality Assurance/Control for National Highway works as well 
as Centrally Sponsored Schemes among executive agencies of this Ministry. 
62.  Accordingly, Quality zone has issued detailed guidelines and Standard Operating 
Procedure for Quality Control/Assurance in construction of National Highways and other 
centrally sponsored projects vide circular dated 01.10.2020 in which it is delegated that 
Quality Control Zone may select any project of the Ministry/NHAI/NHIDCL/BRO on 
random basis to inspect the records/documents related to quality control/assurance & may 
also carry out certain tests in the presence of stakeholders to check the quality of the 
National Highways. Based on such inspection of Quality Control Zone, 
instructions/suggestions will be issued to th e PIUs/ PWD Divisions/ RO Offices for 
necessary compliance. 
63. In compliance to the above, Quality Control Zone has inspected 17 nos. of NHAI/PWD 
Projects in the States of Haryana, Madhya Pradesh, Uttar Pradesh, Andhra Pradesh and 
Jharkhand and have issued instructions/ suggestion to stakeholders. 
64. The Committee takes note of  the various initiatives taken by the Ministry/NHAI to 
ensure good quality in the road infrastructure projects. The Committee, however, 
feels that the existing quality of roads leave a lot to be desired and need more 
stringent quality check mechanisms to ensure high quality construction of roads 
across the country , with specific reference to levelings and smoothness, and also to 
ensure use of standardized and world -class equipment, technology and know-how to 
ensure relevant friction, sloping and gradient to allow rain water to flow out and 
side margin for road safety. In order to prevent road accidents due to drowsiness of 
drivers on long routes, rumble strips should be installed at appropria te places/road 
intersections.  
65. The Committee recommends that random checks for construction & material 
quality and the compliance of mandatory guidelines, may be made by NHAI for all 
its road projects, in addition to the checks made by the approving offici als. Any 
discrepancies/ deficiencies found in the same, should result in disciplinary action 
against the person/ agencies involved in preparing DPR, the concessionaire as well 
as the approving official. The Committee feels that connivance of the approving 

25 
 
authorities with the concessionaire might be the major cause of below par quality of 
construction in National Highways projects across the country. The Committee, 
therefore, recommends that the Ministry may introduce necessary checks and 
balances in order to ensure that the approving authorities as well as the 
concessionaire are accountable for their work, till a stipulated period of time, even 
after the completion of the project.

121. The Committee takes note of the various initiatives taken/being take n by the 
Ministry to address the issue of road safety in the country. The statistics give a 
snapshot regarding road accidents in the country to suggest  that although there is a 
consistent increase in the number of persons getting killed in road accidents, the 
number of road accidents taking place is witnessing a decrease. The Committee is 
apprehensive whether the trend  indicates a decrease in the reporting of road 
accidents across the country or the severity of the road accidents occurring in the 
country has increased over time. The Committee finds that a significant percentage 
of these deaths belongs to  working age individuals  which might be pushing the 
livelihood of many families at stake, causing serious financial trouble/ poverty . The 
Committee recommends the Ministry to target zero accidents on account of faults in 
road design and construction. The Ministry should take up identification and 
rectification of black spots on a war footing, across the country. The Committee 


44 
 
further recommends the Ministry to  conduct research and analyze into why these 
black spots existed in the road projects in the first place and how the same can be 
avoided from the DPR preparation stage itself in the upcoming projects of the 
Ministry. 
122. The Committee takes note of the 2021 World Bank Report titled “Traffic Crash 
Injuries and Disabilities: The Burden on Indian Society”  which st ates that India 
tops the world in road crash deaths, contributing to 11% of all road accident deaths 
worldwide, despite accounting for only 1% of the world’s vehicles. The 2019 World 
Bank Report “Guide for Road Safety Opportunities and Challenges: Low - and 
Middle-Income Countries Country Profiles” estimates the road crash and serious 
injury cost estimate at 7.5% of India’s GDP. The Committee is of the considered 
view that the observations made in World Bank Report should serve as a stark 
reminder of the gra vity of the situation and a sense of urgency with which the 
Ministry should flag Road Safety as top priority, right from  the DPR stage of a NH 
project. 
123. World Bank Report further highlights that  as high as 44% of the households in 
rural areas reported at least one death after a road crash, compared to 11.6% of the 
households in urban areas. Similarly, Low Income Households reported twice the 
number of deaths post-crash vis-à-vis High Income Households. The Committee feels 
that this striking difference might be because of the difference in the quality of 
medical care available to the victims of road accidents. The Committee recommends 
that the Ministry should work in close coordination with the Ministry of Health and 
Family Welfare, to ensure that free quality medical help is provided to road accident 
victims belonging to Low-Income Households. The Committee recommends that this 
may be partially funded by the penalties collected for the violation of traffic Rules. 
124. The Committee recommends that the Ministry may develop a Road Safety score 
to quantify the safety of the National Highways across the country. The ongoing 
projects of the Ministry may be granted approval only if they score excellent in 
terms of Road Safety. The Committee further recommends that the Min istry may 
prescribe a standard format of data to be collected by the concerned local 
authorities. The data thus obtained, may be tapped into in order to gain actionable 
insights into the factors causing road accidents.

accident helpline number 1033 at toll booths and other suitable sites on the NHs, so

that the Ministry may come up with Rules, to fix the accountability of the personnel 
responsible for drafting the Detailed Project Report, till a stipulated period of time,

169. The Ministry, in its written reply, has stated that the policy of this Ministry is n ot to 
permit erection of check barriers on National Highways except where Ministry's prior 
approval is obtained. Check barriers on National Highways, can be provided only in the 
following two situations: 
(i)  Where permission of the Ministry has been obtained for erection of such barriers; and 
(ii)  Temporary barriers erected in emergent situations like maintenance of law and order or 
natural calamities, like, floods, earthquake, etc

check barriers on National Highways needs better implementation, since the 
presence of check barriers on NHs is almost ubiquitous across the country. The 
Committee may be apprised of the steps taken by the Ministry to ensure the 
implementation of this Policy of the Ministry in its true spirit, so as to prevent 
frequent occurrence of traffic jams because of the check barriers.

171. The Ministry, in its written reply, has stated th at the Ministry has been earmarking 
4.3% of Annual Capital Outlay under Tribal Sub Plan (TSP) component, wherein specific 
NH/ road projects are being developed which are fully confined within one or more tribal 
districts. In such cases, development of NH corridors covering specific regions (i.e., tribal 
districts) are being taken up and these projects are not spilling over to other non -tribal 
districts. However, it is not feasible to adopt this approach for dedicated earmarking of 
funds under Scheduled Cast es Sub Plan (SCSP) component, as neither development of 
NHs nor earmarking of funds for NH projects is feasible to specifically benefit any 
specific category/ community. It is not feasible to develop NH projects in tune with 
specific beneficiary oriented s chemes. Accordingly, on number of occasions, through 
various correspondences, it was requested to NITI Aayog, Department of Economic 
Affairs and Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment (M/o SJ&E) that the Ministry 
may be fully exempted from mandatory earmarking of funds under SCSP components.      
172.  The Department related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Transport, 
Tourism and Culture also endorsed MoRT&H’s views for exemption from earmarking 

60 
 
funds under SCSP [Reference para 212 of 278 th Report on Demands for Grants (2020-21) 
of MoRT&H]. 
173.  NITI Aayog, in consultation with Ministry of Finance, had requested the M/o 
SJ&E to take the final decision on exception to any Ministry/ Department.

8.3% of outlay (i.e., about ₹ 8,000 crore) from its overall BE 2021-22 outlay of ₹1,18,101 
crore as these would constrain targets for construction of 12,000 km length of National 
Highways in 2021 -22 and compromise target market borrowing of ₹ 65,000 crore by 
NHAI under IEBR leading to delay in implementation of Major Flagship schemes such as

Highways in this regard and recommends that the Ministry of Finance and Ministry 
of Social Justice and Empowerment may grant special exemption to MoRTH from 
earmarking a part of the allocated funds for SC  welfare. The Committee may be 
apprised about the response received in this regard from MoSJ&E, DEA and NITI 
Aayog.

stakeholders on issues related to Road, Travel & Hospitality sectors; and the officials of 
Ministry of Road Transport and Highways, NHAI, UT Government of Jammu & Kashmir 
on ‘Role of Highways in Nation Building’ with reference to the status of National 
Highways/ State Highways in Jammu and Kashmir.

focus on the maintenance of roads in the Jammu and Kashmir region, since the

Impact of vehicle overloading on National Highways 
181. During a meeting o f the Committee held on 7 th January, 2021 with various 
stakeholders on the subject ‘Role of Highways in Nation Building’, some of the Members 
of the Committee raised the issue of overloading trucks causing damage on roads which 
are not built to withstand such heavy loads. 
182. The Committee recommends that the Ministry may look into the significant 
impact of vehicle overloading on the condition of National Highways across the 
country. The Committee recommends that the Ministry may employ weigh -in-
motion system a t its toll booths across the country, to identify the extent of 
overloading by heavy vehicles, compared to the permitted load which may be 
obtained through FASTag data of the vehicle and impose suitable penalty 
automatically, so as to have a strong detrime ntal effect on truck owners. The 
Committee feels that this will tackle the possible connivance of RTO officials with 
the truck owners for allowing such overloading, and will help in better maintenance 
of National Highways. There should be a special check o n overloaded trucks, 
especially with reference to those transporting goods – stone chips and other 
minerals, causing damage to the roads. 
Setting up Dedicated Underground Utility Corridors 
183. In the meeting of the Committee held on 15 th February, 2021 on Exam ination of 

62 
 
Demands for Grants (2021 -22) of the Ministry, one of the Members raised the issue of 
frequent trenching of roads across the country for the purpose of Namami Gange project, 
laying of gas pipelines, optical fibers, telephone lines etc. He suggest ed the creation of 
utility corridors which can be utilized for such services to prevent frequent trenching of 
roads. He further suggested the monetization of the utility corridors through the creation 
of a company under the Ministry. 
184. The Committee is of th e view that roads across the country require frequent 
trenching for the purpose of laying of fiber lines, gas pipelines, and other similar 
amenities. The patchwork done thereafter is often delayed and rarely meets the 
desired construction quality, thus thw arting the speed of vehicles on the road and 
acting as a safety hazard. The Committee recommends that the Ministry may 
consider the inclusion of a provision for dedicated underground utility corridors in 
its upcoming National Highways projects to prevent f requent trenching.  The 
provision for construction of dedicated underground utility corridor should be 
included at the DPR stage itself.  The extra cost incurred for building the 
underground utility corridors may be replenished by monetizing the constructed 
utility corridors by charging the Departments and Companies which will benefit 
from avoidance of frequent trenching of roads. The Committee recommends that the 
Ministry may create a Special Purpose Vehicle (SPV) for the purpose of 
monetization of the utility corridors.

pandemic

Atmanirbhar Bharat, for providing relief to Contractors/ Devel opers/ Concessionaires of 
Road Sector from the impact of COVID, subsequent lockdown and other measures taken 
to prevent spread of COVID.

development of roads in the country. The Committee further recommends that the

and improve the state of Road Safety in the country. The Committee, would like the
