CHAPTER-I 
 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS WHICH HAVE BEEN ACCEPTED BY 
THE MINISTRY 
 
DEMANDS FOR GRANTS (2021-22) OF THE MINISTRY 
Recommendation/Observation 
1. The Committee understands that many of the programmes / schemes relating to Port 
modernization, Port infrastructure development, ship building, ship repairing and inland 
waterways transport are lagging behind because of the drastic cuts effected and would 
ultimately lead to both time and cost overruns. The Committee is of the view that if the 
Ministry wants adequate/ substantial budgetary support to complete its projects, the pace of 
implementation of the projects will have to be spruced up and the allocate d funds be 
optimally utilized. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Ministry should initiate 
and implement measures for better financial discipline and ensure that the scarce resources do 
not remain locked up and surrendered later on.  
                   (Para 6) 
Reply of Ministry 
1.1 Noted for necessary compliance. In this connection, necessary instructions in 
compliance of above recommendations/directions of the Hon’ble Committee have been 
issued by IWAI vide O.M. dated 23.08.2021 to all concerned. 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
2. The Committee would like the Ministry to ensure effective coordination among the 
Central Line Ministries, State Governments/ State Maritime Boards and SPVs for 
implementation of projects earmarked under the Sagarmala Programme and constitute a 
Committee to encourage convergence at Central and State level and also to sort out various 
inter-Ministerial issues at the Central level as well as the issues with the States and other 
stakeholders. Since there is a huge difference between the projected demand and all ocated 
funds, the Committee would advise the Ministry to implement effective measures to 

3 
  
optimally utilize the allocated resources instead of keeping a vast chunk of its resources 
locked up and surrender them towards the end of financial year.  
                  (Para 11) 
Reply of Ministry 
2.1 The recommendation of the Committee has been noted. 
2.2 It is mentioned that as per Cabinet mandate a National Sagarmala Apex Committee 
(NSAC) has been constituted for overall policy guidance and high level coordinati on, and to 
review various aspects of planning and implementation of the plan and projects. 
2.3 A Sagarmala Coordination and Steering Committee (SCSC) was constituted under the 
chairmanship of the Cabinet Secretary with Port, Shipping & Waterways (formally Ministry 
of Shipping), Road Transport and Highways, Tourism, Defence, Home Affairs, Environment, 
Forest & Climate Change, Department of Revenue, Expenditure, Industrial Policy and 
Promotion, Chairman, Railway Board and CEO, NITI Aayog as members. 
2.4 Three meetings conducted under the chairmanship of the Cabinet Secretary dated 1 st 
October 2015, 4 th April 2016 and 25 th November 2016. As recommended in 3 rd meeting of 
SCSC, major responsibilities related to projects identified in NPP and Master Planning of 
Major Ports were allocated to MoPSW.

Estimates and Actual Expenditure had, in its 279 th Report on Demands for Grants (2020 -21)

requirements and exercise due diligence in its Budget formulation after proper assessment 
and planning. The Committee, is theref ore, constrained to note the failure of the Ministry to 
fully utilize the budgeted funds under various heads during 2020 -21. For instance, Rs 211.00 
crores were allocated at the stage of BE 2020 -21 under the head “Sagarmala Schemes and 
Projects” which got reduced to Rs 96.69 crores at the RE stage whereas the actual 
expenditure incurred till 05.02.2021 is only Rs 74.92 crores. Similarly, ship building which is

“Assistance to Ship Building, Research and 71 Development” from BE of Rs 151.00 crores

roughly 25% has remained unspent. Under the head “Grants to Inland Water Transport 
Authority of India”, a sum of Rs 301.80 crores was proposed in BE 2020 -21, which got 
reduced to Rs 203.20 crores at the RE stage. However, the Ministry was able to spend o nly

all the projects under various heads and address the bottlenecks arising during the

10.2 Digital initiative for Maritime Training Institutes and Seafarers  
Three-Tier Mechanism of training: 
The Directorate introduced a Three-Tier Mechanism of training leading to issuance of 
a Certificate of Proficiency or a Course Completion Certificate vide DGS Order 20 of 
2020 dated 04.08.2020. 
It was found that each MTI with its own mechanism of assessment of competency 
may result in variation of output quality and i ts resultant impact on Indian seafarers. 
The Directorate devised a Three -Tier Mechanism of Training for achievement or 
maintenance of competency to ensure certain standardization of quality of output 
from all approved MTI. The Three Tiers of this mechanism  for a particular STCW 
Courses comprise of E -Learning course (approved by Directorate) to be completed 
and passed by a seafarer from comfort of his home, a course comprising of practical 
and theoretical component to be completed by each seafarer at an appr oved MTI and 
finally, a seafarer need to pass an on -line exam called EXIT Exam with the issuance 
of the digitally signed certificates. 
E-learning module: 
E-learning platform was developed for the candidates to access study material for the 
certificate of competency examinations for various grades and STCW Modular 
Courses. E -learning material is provided at no cost to the candidates. E -learning 
would help the candidates to improve their learning and performance in the 
examinations, to improve the quality of  officers and ensure their employability. The 
total number of candidates registered for the e-Learning till date is 704761. 
Virtual Classes: 
The DGS has allowed Maritime Training Institutes to conduct Classes for approved 
maritime courses by the use of Dig ital technologies for Virtual Classes/ Live Video 
Sessions during COVID -19 pandemic. The approved Institutes register the qualified 
students for their courses as per STCW requirements and conducts online courses 
without compromising on the course hours req uired for all competencies. Video 
recordings on each class is maintained for record and verification purposes and once 
course is  completed online, students are permitted to appear for the online common 
exit exam.  

12 
  
Online EXIT Exam: 
An online EXIT examination for the STCW modular courses was started to bring out 
a uniform methodology required to carry out assessment of a candidate for the desired 
competency. Total number of seafarers who appeared for online EXIT Exam are 
5,17,383 out of which 4,69,187 passed.  
Digitally signed certificates: 
The Directorate issued guidelines for digitally signed certificates for successfully 
completing maritime courses conducted by Maritime Training Institutes vide the 
Training Circular 21 of 2020 dated 27.05.2020.  
It was fo und that there was a need to have the transparency and uniformity in the 
certificates issued and to make it convenient for the verifying authority to verify them, 
therefore, Directorate introduced the digitally signed certificates. The e -Governance 
system of the Directorate has issued 3,71,655 digital maritime course e-certificates.

A.  The number of oil spill incidents that took place in the last five years: 03 (Three). 
B.    The details of the steps taken for prevention of the same: 
 Following are the steps in regards to prevention oil spills from ships: 
a. Annex 1 of MARPOL convention, to which India is party to, deals with Prevention 
of Pollution by Oil. The aforesaid convention, besides mandating the construction and 
operational requirement for ships to prevent pollution by oil, also specifies the 
requirements for emergency response in case of oil spill. Indian ships are surveyed at 
periodic intervals to ensure compliance with the requirement of the MARPOL 
Convention. 
b. In addition, to discourage operati on of sub -standard vessels in Indian water, Flag 
State Inspections (FSI) and Port State Control (PSC) Inspections of ships in Indian 
ports are carried out to ensure compliance of ships with applicable regulation, for 
prevention of pollution by oil. 
c. Nati onal response mechanism to deal with oil spill incidents has been prepared 
(NOS-DCP). 

23 
  
d. Merchant Shipping (Regulations of Entry of Ships into Ports, Anchorages and 
Offshore facilities) Rules, 2012 has provisions that require older vessels to conform to 
the standards of members of the Association of International Classification Societies 
and also all vessels calling at Indian  Ports are required to carry insurance against oil 
spills under Civil Liability    Convention and Limitation of Liability Convention et c, 
so that possibility of oil-spill from such vessel is minimized. 
e. Coast Guard has been designated as the nodal authority to combat oil spills in 
Indian waters. All major ports have also been equipped to handle minor oil spills in 
their waters. 
f. In ad dition, India is a member of International Oil Pollution Convention Funds 
(IOPC Funds) which provides compensation in the event of oil pollution if the amount 
of compensation exceeds the CLC/LLMC limits to deal with compensation matters in 
case of an oil-spill from certain types of oil.  
g. Further, 'Traffic separation scheme' have been promulgated in West coast of India, 
off Cochin and Lakshadweep islands, to avoid collisions of the vessels, which might 
lead to severe oil pollution cases.

Recommendation/Observation   
5. The Committee notes the reply of the Ministry regarding the values of parameters of 
Average Turn-around time and Average Output Per Ship Berthday at Major Ports across the 
country. The Committee is not aware about its competitiveness when compared with oth er 
Ports of the world. The Committee is of the view that the performance of a Port is not solely 
dependent on these parameters but also on other factors such as manpower supply and regular 
supply chain. The Committee would urge the Ministry to develop an e fficient system which 
can address these inadequacies and also support seamless movement of cargo across all 
modes. The Ministry should emphasize all the Major and Minor Ports to enhance the 

32 
  
productivity and infrastructure to the level of best Ports in the world which will enable them 
to compete globally.           
(Para 36) 
Reply of Ministry 
5.1 Ministry of Ports, Shipping and Waterways have been focussing on interventions 
which would streamline the EXIM process and help in reducing dwell time and transacti on 
costs at the Major Ports. Initiatives such as Direct Port Entry and Direct Port Delivery, and 
the Radio Frequency Identification system and Port Community System (PCS), were all 
aimed at reducing the time and cost of clearance of goods. 
 
5.2 One of the key measures towards EXIM procedure is Direct Port Entry (DPE) and 
Direct Port Delivery (DPD). The percentage of DPD has increased from 5.42% in April -2016 
to 61.19% in March, 2021. The facility of DPE is well received by trade and the percentage 
of containers cleared under DPE is 46.44% in financial year 2020-21. 
 
5.3 As far as the creation of paperless trading environment is concerned, major strides 
have been taken at the Major Ports towards the digitization of key EXIM processes. The PCS 
1x has digitized  processes such as Electronic Invoice (e -Invoice), Electronic Payment (e -
Payment) and Electronic Delivery Order (e -DO) for physical release of cargo by custodians. 
Further, the process of generation of electronic Bill of Lading (e -BL) and enabling the Lett er 
of Credit (LC) process to be conducted digitally have already been implemented in the PCS 
1x. Uploading of documents by the importers and exporters is done on e -SANCHIT (e -
Storage and Computerized Handling of Indirect Tax Documents) launched by CBIC. 
Electronic communication of Out of Charge (OOC), Bill of Entry and gate -pass to 
importers/customs brokers has been enabled in the Indian Customs EDI Gateway 
(ICEGATE). Further, the Radio Frequency Identification Device (RFID) solution has been 
implemented at  all Major Ports to enable seamless movement of traffic across port gates, 
including substantial reductions in documentation checks. All Major Ports have already 
implemented Radio Frequency Identification Device (RFID). Upgradation and integration 
with recent technologies- IoT, Blockchain to ease transaction and real time basis tracking has 
been envisaged in Maritime India Vision 2030. 
5.4 Moreover, to streamline the process of scanning and reduce the time for scanning and 
checking of containers, 8 Mobile X -ray Container Scanners (in addition to existing 4 X -ray 

33 
  
container scanners previously installed by customs) have been installed recently at various 
Major Ports. 
5.5 The aforementioned measures have had considerable positive impact in the trade 
ecosystem. Key operational metrics have displayed overall improvement in 2020 -21 as 
compared to 2019 -20. The overall average pre -berthing time (under port account) has 
reduced from 7.23 hours in April -March 2020 to 5.57 hours in April -March 2021. Further , 
overall average turnaround time (under port account) improved from 49.38 hours in April -
March 2020 to 46.69 hours in April-March 2021.

DREDGING ACTIVITIES  
Recommendation/Observation  
10. The Committee is of the view that Port development requires safe tidal windows for 
navigation, sufficient berthing space and depth and acceptable conditions for operations on 
the berth. The Committee suggests that the Ministry should adopt advanced dredging 
strategies such as maintaining local and regional sediment levels, recharging salt  marsh areas

restoration/creation or ecological enhancement of Port structures. The Committee also wishes 

37 
  
to point out that the cost of maintenance of dredging varies  at each Port while the average 
cost is at around Rs. 10 crores, It is at the highest level at SMP Kolkata, Deendayal and

Reply of Ministry  
10.1 Dredging work is undertaken by the Port based on the littoral drift and sedimentation 
pattern either during pre -monsoon or post -monsoon except SMP Kolkata, Cochin and 
Deendayal Port wherein due to the estuary/riverine port requires continuous dredging is 
required throughout the year. 
10.2 Dredging cost is dependent on the dredging volume and quantities vis-à-vis the 
haulage distance to dumping ground, therefore the dredging project cost varies between ports. 
10.3 The Syama Prasad Mookerjee Port, Kolkata is a riverine  port subjected to heavy 
siltation. The Deendayal Port located in creek is also subjected to heavy siltation by natural 
phenomena. The JNPT is subjected to heavy siltation in the channel due to littoral drift. 
Hence, the maintenance dredging with high volu me is necessary. However, the Ports are 
taking steps to bring down the cost of dredging. 
10.4 Dredging activities are governed by Environment clearance and all the dredging 
projects adhere to preservation of eco-system and ecology. 
10.5 The SMP Kolkata, De endayal Port and Jawaharlal Nehru Port have been adopting 
steps for reducing the dredging cost which are as follows :- 
i. Timely hydrographic survey of the channel, turning circle, basin etc., for 
identifying optimal dredging requirements; 
ii. Undertaking studies on the behavior of the channel for siltation erosion and other 
natural phenomenon; 
iii. Deployment of suitable dredgers with adequate hopper capacity for reducing the 
cost and time for the project; 
iv. To reuse the dredge material for various activities including beach nourishment, 
construction activities etc., where feasible, thus reducing the cost of dredging

Recommendation/Observation 
1. The Committee observes that allocation made to the Ministry for FY 2021 -22 is 45 
percent less than the projected demand and the shortfall between the projected demand of Rs. 
3101.34 crore and the Budget Estimates of Rs. 1702.5 for the Ministry of Shipping is to the 
tune of Rs. 1398.95 crore, which is massive by any standards and is certain to have an 
adverse bearing on the implementation of various modernization projects of the Ministry. 
Major reduction has been effected under Sagarmala Schemes and Projects  and other schemes 
under Sagarmala in the Revenue section. The same is the case with Grants to Inland Water 
Transport Authority of India, D.G. Shipping and Kolkata Port Trust. This being the case, the 
Committee is convinced that it would be an insurmountab le task for the Ministry to 
efficiently run a flagship scheme like Sagarmala and other schemes under Sagarmala with 
this limited allocation and achieve goals envisaged under Sagarmala Scheme. The Committee 
further notes a steep cut in allocation to IWAI an d D.G. Shipping, the two important offices 
of the Ministry. The Committee apprehends that the working of these two offices may get 
hampered due to less allocation. The Committee further notes that on the capital expenditure 
of DG Shipping, against a sum of  Rs. 108.4 crore sought, only Rs. 25 crore has been 
allocated. The Ministry submitted that due to this inadequate allocation, the priority project of 
e-Governance will suffer. In this era of digital technology, where the Government has been 
emphasizing for moving towards digitization, less allocation to e -Governance project is not 
acceptable. The Committee observes that India has been emerging as a modern economy and 

42 
  
successive Governments have targeted to increase the economic growth at a high rate in a 
sustained manner. However, the COVID -19 pandemic has had a disruptive impact on the 
Indian economy and almost all the sectors have been adversely affected. The Committee is of 
the view that post -COVID, the economic growth of the country will come through Ind ia’s 
Port and shipping sector because Maritime Transport is a critical infrastructure for the 
economic growth as 95% of the country’s trade by volume and 68% by value is moved 
through Maritime Transport and the ports and shipping sector is, thus, a key dri ver of trade 
for India. Keeping all the above facts  in view, the Committee is of the considered opinion 
that the outlay of Rs. 1702.35 crore would not be sufficient to meet the fund requirements of 
the Ministry during 2021 -22. The Committee, therefore, re commends that the Ministry

Ministry of Finance for augmentation of financial resources for it for 2021 -22 at RE stage.

Realizing the fact that our ports and shipping sector is a key driver of trade for our

recommendation has been “noted for necessary compliance” is not sufficient. The 
Committee feels that the notable reduction in allocation made at B.E. 2021 -22 stage, in

made by the Ministry for the FY 2021 -22. The Committee would, therefore, like to 
know the al location made to the Ministry at the R.E. 2021 -22 stage. In case no 
significant budgetary enhancement has been made, the Committee may be apprised of

The Committee while making its recommendati on in Para 17 of its 290 th Report had 
inter alia intended that the Ministry should pay more attention to improvement of port 
productivity and port operations through modernization of port infrastructure and 
adoption of sophisticated technology. Instead of dwelling upon the measures taken in 
this regard, the Ministry seems to have washed its hands off the matter by stating that 
Non-Major Ports are under the control of State Maritime Boards or State 
Governments. The Committee observes that India has not been able to reap the full 
potential of its port and shipping sector which is evident from the fact that the 
contribution of this sector to our GDP is just 1%. The Committee, therefore, desires to 
be apprised of the policy measures initiated to overcome structural and organizational 
impediments to increase port production and productivity. Considering the fact that the 
number of Minor Ports in the country is more than 200 and therefore, their role in the

CHAPTER-I 
 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS WHICH HAVE BEEN ACCEPTED BY 
THE MINISTRY 
Airport Infrastructure  
Recommendation/Observation  
1. The Committee notes that the aviation industry in India has witnessed tremendous 
amount of growth over the last decade as is eviden t from the fact that India’s domestic 
passenger throughput has reached around 137 million in FY 2019 -20 from 61 million in FY 
2013-14 and international passenger traffic has reached 67 million in FY 2019 -20 from 47 
million in FY 2013 -14. Prior to the outbr eak of COVID -19 pandemic, the Indian civil 
aviation sector was growing at a CAGR of 14% and was among the fastest growing civil 
aviation sector in the world. Despite India being the world’s fastest growing aviation market, 
its airports are grappling with s erious capacity constraints because such a pace of growth 
has resulted in a strain on the aviation infrastructure, resulting in traffic congestions and 
delays at majority of the airports. If a high growth in civil aviation sector is to be sustained, 
it is imperative to augment and modernize India’s aviation infrastructure. The Committee 
notes with satisfaction that the AAI and private airport operators have envisaged a 
modernization and development plan with an estimated cost of ₹89,000 crore by 2024. The 
Committee urges the Ministry to make privacy a focus of the regulatory framework for the 
Ecosystem of Drones. 
(Para 7.5) 
Reply of the Ministry 
1.1 Ministry of Civil Aviation has notified liberalized Drone Rules 2021 on 25 August 
2021. The Rules are based on  trust, self -certification and non -intrusive monitoring. The 
essential features include: 
a) Every drone, except for those meant for research, development and testing 
purposes, is required to be registered and should have a Unique Identification Number 
(UIN). 
b) An airspace map of the country segregating the entire airspace into red, yellow 
and green zones is available on the digital sky platform. Operation of drones in red and 
yellow zones is subject to the approval of Central Government and Airports Au thority 
of India (AAI) respectively. No approval is required for operation of drones in green 
zones. 
c) The State Government, the Union Territory Administration and Law 
enforcement agencies have been empowered under the Rules to declare a temporary red 
zone for a specified period. 

3 
 
d) Drones are required to have the necessary type certification issued by 
Directorate General of Civil Aviation (DGCA). No type certification is however 
required in case of nano drones (up to 250 gram all -up weight) and model drones made 
for research and recreation purpose. 
e) The owner and operators of drones are required to furnish the necessary 
personal details including their Indian passport number etc. for issuance of any 
registration or licence. 
f) Rule 17 of the Drone Rules, 2021, lays down the provision of transfer of drone 
to another person by way of sale, lease, gift or any other mode, after providing requisite 
details of the transferor, transferee and unique identification number of the drone on the 
digital sky platform along with the applicable fees. 
g) Drone operations that violate the provisions of the Drone Rules, 2021 are 
punishable under Rule 49 of the Drone Rules, 2021 as well as provisions of any other 
law, for the time being in force. 
Recommendation/Observation  
2. The Committee urges upon the Ministry to develop a comprehensive, strategic and 
futuristic Master Plan for implementation of projects to provide world class airport 
infrastructure, by bringing in cutting edge technology and the global best practices o f the 
aviation industry, so as to encourage growth in passenger and cargo traffic and catapult 
India into the league of top aviation markets within a period of 5 years. The Committee 
would like the Ministry to address not only the existing capacity constra ints in various 
airports, but also address infrastructural requirements in the context of growth scenario 
forecast for the coming years. It should be strictly ensured that the development/ upgradation 
of airport projects are completed as per the prescribed timelines. 
(Para 7.6) 
Reply of the Ministry 
2.1 All Airports are being comprehensively planned and developed considering long term 
forecast.  Accordingly, land is earmarked / additional land is requested from State 
Government based on long -term futuristic development of single runway or parallel runway 
configurations and the type of aircraft expected to operate in future considering the potential 
of traffic it will be handling.  Due to the dynamic nature of development, the Master Plans are 
reviewed regularly based on the revised growth forecast. The expansion of development of 
infrastructure facilities at the airports is a continuous process and is undertaken on the 
operational requirements for safety of aircraft operation and demand from airlines, dependi ng 
upon availability of land and viability, as well as other facilities with reference to intended 
aircraft operations. To create additional capacity, work is in progress at Goa, Port Blair, 
Agartala, Guwahati, Chennai, Lucknow, Dehradun, Leh, Trichy, Pune , Patna, Darbhanga 
(CE), Kolhapur, Bareilly (CE), Jabalpur, Surat, Adampur (CE), Kanpur (CE), Bhubaneshwar, 
Vijayawada etc.  Work is in planning stage at Jaipur, Srinagar, Agra, Indore, Ahmedabad, 

4 
 
Bihta (CE), Bhubaneshwar, Varanasi etc. AAI is not just building new Greenfield airports but 
is also upgrading its airside infrastructure with works like runway extension, strengthening 
and resurfacing of runways, construction of parallel taxiways, rapid exit taxiways, ATC 
Tower cum Technical block, setting up adequate ground installations like Instrument Landing 
System (ILS), DVOR, ASR/MSSR etc.418 additional parking bays are planned at various 
airports in next five years for night parking of new aircrafts being purchased by airline 
operators.  The list of additio nal parking bays (proposed / under construction) is enclosed as 
Annexure A. Route optimization, CDO (Continuous Descent Operation), Upper Airspace 
harmonization, ATM Automation, Flexible Use of Airspace, R&D, Telecommunication 
Infrastructure upgradation, A utomation system backup, Remote Tower and alternate towers, 
Procurement of aircraft for FIU, Replacement of CNS facilities, etc. are other initiates which 
are taken up at airports for making these upto date. 
Recommendation/Observation  
3. The Committee als o urges the Ministry to ensure that adequate parking space and 
slots are available at the airports. The Committee notes that potential growth in the 
passenger and cargo traffic would require enormous investments in terms of construction of 
new airports and  expansion and modernization of existing airports. Given the risks, lenders 
are cautious about issuing long -term debt to airport operators. The Committee, therefore, 
would like the Ministry to formulate necessary policies, schemes and guidelines, to attrac t 
much needed investment for airport projects so that the way for raising resources towards 
funding the development, modernization and upgradation plans of airports could be paved 
and multiple funding option including external commercial borrowing, capital  markets long-
term borrowing etc. could be explored.

Air Cargo  
Recommendation/Observation  
6. The Committee notes that besides geographical location, India’s cargo industry has 
the advantage of a growing economy along with a population of 1.3 billion plus India’s 
impressive growth in international and domestic trade in the last decade. However, despit e 
tremendous potential, India’s total annual freight volumes stood at 3.33 MMT in fiscal 2019 -
20 and has not reached close to any one of the top three world -class airports, viz., Hong 
Kong, Memphis and Shanghai. The Committee is constrained to note that th e total air cargo 
throughput handled by all Indian airports put together is less than that handled by individual 
airports like Hong Kong, Memphis and Shanghai. It is, therefore, evidently clear that despite 
having all the ingredients to be one of the world’s air cargo hubs, India has not fully realized 
its potential in terms of air cargo. The Committee is of the view that inadequate 
infrastructure is a major bottleneck in developing the country’s air cargo sector. The 
Committee, therefore, recommends that the Ministry should take effective steps to address the 
crippling infrastructure constraints by way of establishing dedicated cargo airports in the 
country and developing new airports with a focus on making them cargo hubs so that the 
Ministry’s ambitious cargo throughput target of 10 MMT by 2027 could be realized.

Reply of the Ministry 
6.1 The observations of Hon’ble Committee have been noted. In this regard, the following 
submissions are relevant:

export cargo processed through Air Cargo Terminals. 
● In Indian Customs scenario, majority of the consignments for import and export ar e 
subjected to Customs examination/inspection, whereas in the foreign Airports under 
reference, very few consignments are subjected for examination/inspection. 
● So far as the setting up of dedicated cargo airports is concerned, it may be noted that 
this option would be feasible if there is critical minimum level of cargo is available 
for air transportation. Presently, establishment of dedicated cargo airports in India is 
not feasible on account of following: 
⮚ Current tonnage handling capacity in India is alre ady around double the cargo 
presently handled at various terminals in India. 

7 
 
⮚ Bulk of air cargo handled in India as Belly cargo in passenger aircrafts 
whereas in other countries most of the cargo is transported in dedicated 
freighter aircraft. 
⮚ India has too few dedicated freighter aircraft as compared to other countries. 
⮚ There is less trans -shipment cargo handled in India as compared to other 
countries. 
● Hong Kong, Memphis and Shanghai model are different from India’s model as they 
are primarily Trans-shipment based Air Cargo Terminals.

Airport Infrastructure  
Recommendation/Observation

structure of airports and the way the airport concessions are given. At present, the rights to

Recommendation/Observation  
13. Land acquisition is a major problem due to land scarcity and huge capital 
requirement. The Committee feels that there are many regional airports which can be 
developed by States on their own or in collaboration with the Airports Authority of India 
(AAI) and that the State Governments should explore the setting up of “no-frill airports”.

Reply of the Ministry 
13.1 Government of India (GoI) has formulated a Greenfield Airports (G FA) Policy, 2008 
which provides guidelines, procedure and conditions for establishment of new Greenfield 
Airports in the country. As per Policy, an airport developer, including the State Government, 
willing to establish an airport is required to send a pro posal to the Ministry of Civil Aviation 
(MoCA). There is a 2-stage process for approval of the proposal i.e., 'Site Clearance' and 'In -
Principle' approval stage. In accordance with this policy, MoCA receives proposals from the 
State Governments or Airport Developers from time to time for establishment of airports. 
After due examination, the approval for development of a new Greenfield Airport is granted. 
The responsibility of implementation of airport project including funding of the project rests 
with the concerned airport developer. Generally, land for airport projects is provided by 
concerned State Government/ Union Territory (UT) Administration to AAI free of cost and 
free from all encumbrances. As per the AAI Act, in case a State Government wishes to 
facilitate setting up of the airport, it could provide the following incentives to an Airport 
Company: 
(a) land, concessional or otherwise; 

24 
 
(b) real estate development rights in and around the airports; 
(c) airport connectivity; rail, road; 
(d) fiscal incentives by way of exemptions from State taxes; and 
(e) any other assistance that the State Government deem fit. State Governments may 
evolve their respective policies for providing any or all of the aforesaid incentives to an 
Airport Company. If the sel ection of a private entity or JVC partner is to be made by the 
State Government or its entity it shall be done through open competitive bidding. While 
granting land and other benefits, the State Government may, if it deems fit, stipulate the 
rights and obl igations of the Airport Company as conditions of such grant. State 
Governments can also provide land to AAI for development of greenfield airports through 
concessions to be granted to private entities in accordance with the provisions of the AAI 
Act. State s may also provide any of the above concessions to AAI for facilitating the 
development of airports in their respective States.

Recommendation/Observation

The Committee desires to know the impact of the measures undertaken to support the 
Indian MRO sector and the resultant increase, if any, in MRO services. The Committee 
reiterating its recommendation, stresses upon the urgent need for growth in MRO 
services k eeping in view the existing technical manpower, low labour cost and the 
expected growth in the aviation sector.  
(Para 8.3) 
Krishi Udan 
 
The Committee appreciates the steps taken by the Ministry on coordination with seven 
other Ministries/ Departments name ly Department of Agriculture & Farmer’s Welfare; 
Department of Animal Husbandry & Dairying; Department of Fisheries; Ministry of 
Food Processing Industries; Department of Commerce; Ministry of Tribal Affairs; and 
Ministry of Development of North -eastern Re gion (DoNER),  to successfully implement 
the Krishi Udan Scheme for transportation of agri -produce. The Committee desires to 
know the progress of plan to create 33% of more of domestic terminals by FY 2023 -24 
and the increase in volume of cold storages at a irports. The Committee would also desire 
to know the status of implementation of e -Kushal (Krishi Udan for Sustainable Holistic 
Agri Logistics) and the result of planned collaboration with the stakeholders.   
(Para 9.3) 
Connectivity to North East and other remote areas 
 
The Committee has time and again stressed upon the need for increasing connectivity at 
inaccessible locations in the NER, especially the Hollongi Airport in Arunachal Pradesh. 

61 
 
The Committee notes that work of a new Greenfield airport at Hollongi is in progress and 
desires to know the status of work completion and the tentative date to operationalise the 
airport. The Committee also stresses upon the need for renewed efforts in development of 
water aerodromes and heliports as it requires less s pace and less capital as compared to 
airports. 
(Para 10.4) 
Shortage of Pilots 
 
The Committee notes the reply. It also desires specific information regarding the progress 
of establishment of nine FTOs at five airports and the timeline set for it. The Commit tee 
also recommends that a space should be allocated at each airport for the FTOs to enable 
them to keep their training equipments. 
(Para 11.2) 
Aero Club of India 
 
The Committee understands that the Draft aero -sports policy for development of aero -
sports activities in India has been published for public feedback on 1 st January, 2022. The 
Committee is surprised that while the Ministry is replying to the subject, it has not notified 
that the policy has been framed and put for public circulation. Therefore the Committee 
observed that the proposal may be brought over for discussion and recommendation of the 
committee prior to the notification at the policy level. The Committee also took note that 
such policies, which are being formulated by the Government, are approved and 
thereafter subject to examination of the committee w hich is not a reasonable practice. The 
Committee would like to state that the aero -sports policy must be first put up for 
examination of the Standing Committee prior to seeking its recommendation before it is 
notified as a policy. 
(Para 12.5) 
 
13.2 The Committee has taken note of the explanation and it is felt that the real issue has 
not been addressed which relates to issue of allotment of Land by the Ministry of Urban 
Development. The Committee would like to understand that once the nature of allotment 
to the Aero Club of India was in the form of license agreement dated 27.12.1984 which was 
irrecoverable in the nature as specified in section 60 (b) of the Indian Easement Act, 1882. 
The Committee observes that the basic issue of cancellation of allotment of  a license plot 
on which the Aero Club of India has constructed its building as per the norms and the 
Committee does not find justifiable reason for its Cancellation.  
(Para 13.2) 
Carbon Offsetting and Reduction Scheme for International Aviation (CORSIA) 
The Committee stresses upon the need for protecting India’s interests on the adverse 
implication of CORSIA. It approves the proposal of the Ministry to take up the matter at 
diplomatic level through Ministry of External Affairs and hopes that all efforts w ould be 
made to bring on board like -minded developing countries, so that a unified effort can be 
made to review the CORSIA scheme in favour of our country.  
(Para 14.2) 
Cancellation charges 

62 
 
The Committee notes with concern the reply of the Ministry that cancellation charges are 
not regulated by Government, which has resulted in no uniformity in cancellation 
charges levied by different airlines. The Committee feels that it defies logic that fl ights of 
different airlines on a particular sector having the same starting and destination points, 
and where the duration of the flight is also the same, should have different cancellation 
charges. The Committee, therefore, strongly recommends that there should be uniform 
cancellation charges across all airlines.  
(Para 15.2) 
Cancellation or delaying of flights 
 
The Committee notes with appreciation that based on the directions of the Committee, 
the Ministry has issued guidelines to all airlines/ airports to extend facilities to passengers 
in case of cancellation or delay of flights. The Committee would like to be apprised of the 
ground level implementation of the Ministry’s orders and the number of airports and 
airlines which have implemented it and the de tails of facilities extended and the number 
of passengers who have availed the facilities, airport-wise and airlines-wise.  
(Para 16.2) 
Making Airports Accessible to all under the ‘Accessible India Campaign’ 
 
The Committee notes that ‘Accessibility Standards and Guidelines for Civil Aviation’ 
containing all the details on Accessible Airport Infrastructure has been prepared and 
placed in public domain for comments/suggestion by stakeholders after due consultatio n 
with Chief Commissioner of Persons with Disability (CCPD) and that 
comments/suggestions from stakeholders have been deliberated and final guidelines are 
expected by year end. The Committee desires to know the present status of issues of 
guidelines for as sisting the differently abled people and the timeline set for its 
implementation at all airports.  
(Para 17.2) 
Inefficiency of hangars 
 
The Committee desires to know the plans of the Ministry to build well equipped hangars 
at remote places.   
(Para 18.2)

DEVELOPMENT AND CONSERVATION OF MUSEUMS: CHALLENGES AND 
OPPORTUNITIES 
Recommendation/Observation 
 1. The Committee takes note of the steps taken by the Ministry for the upgradation of the 
security infrastructure, Reception Halls, Auditorium etc., with the latest technology. and 
desires that the betterment of the Galleries may be completed at all the Museu ms within a 
fixed timeframe. The Committee strongly recommends that the Museums in India should be 
adequately equipped with conservation labs, storage facilities, written and graphic records, 
documentation facilities, modern photography techniques etc. 
(Para 4.6)  
Reply of Ministry  
 
1.1 National Museum:  National Museum has recently upgraded reception area, CCTV 
infrastructure and auditorium with latest technology. NM has also upgraded 6 halls with latest 
technology. Remaining galleries and storage spaces are being upgraded in phased manner. 
NM has also recently upgraded its Conservation Laboratory. NM has also created digital 
infrastructure for safekeeping on digital record.   
1.2 Indian Museum: - Indian Museum, Kolkata has made the following progress 
pertaining to the upgradation of security infrastructure –  
 CISF personnel have been deployed at the Indian Museum. 
 The Security Surveillance system is operational and is being upgraded further in phases 
within the limitations of fund availability. 
 Door Frame Metal Detectors and Hand Held Metal Detectors are being utilised for 
frisking of visitors. 
 For the convenience of visitors, online ticketing facility has been introduced. 
In addition, approval has been accorded by the Board of Trustees for construction of a new 
building to house modern storage facility of artefacts in the reserve collection of the Museum 
and for setting up of a state -of-the-art conservation and preservation laboratory.  This work 
has been initiated through CPWD.  
1.4 NCSM: - NCSM has 25 centres functioning in different parts of the country. Annual 
action plans are made for the upgradation/ modernization and addition of new galleries using 
latest digital display technolog ies. However, funds are required to take up such works in a 
phased manner. The Central Research & Training Laboratory in Kolkata , which provides 
catalytic support to several institutions in terms of display technologies , requires funds in a 
phase manner to enhance the R&D capability. 

3 
 
1.5 Allahabad Museum: - The security infrastructure of Allahabad Museum has been 
upgraded with round the clock CCTV monitoring. The Conservation Lab of Museum is 
functional and very efficient in functioning. All the record of Museum are being digitalised. 
1.6 Salar Jung Museum: - Salar Jung Museum is already equipped with Security 
Infrastructure, Auditorium and Lecture Halls with latest Audio/video technologies. Salar Jung 
Museum is also equipped with full fledged Conservation Lab and Photography Department, a 
Modern Library and Ma nuscript Library and Digitization equipment and adequate Storage 
facility for Reserve Collections. 
1.7 NGMA: - The National Gallery of Modern Art, New Delhi is already equipped with 
Security Infrastructure, Auditorium and Lecture Halls with latest Audio/vi deo technologies. 
NGMA, New Delhi is also equipped with full -fledged Conservation Lab.  An Art Reference 
Modern Library and Manuscript Library and Digitization equipment and adequate Storage  
facility for Reserve Collections. 
1.8 ASI:- ASI has its own Science branch which is well equipped with latest equipment/ 
technology. As and when required, antiquities from the museums under ASI are sent for 
preservation/ conservation. All museums under ASI have documented the antiquities in site

modifying the existing Legislation/ Rules so that the receipts collected by ASI are not 
deposited in the Consolidated Fund of India but into a special fund dedicated to the 
protection and preservation of historical monuments and sites.  The Committee feels 
that doing so would bridge the gap between the budgetary requirements of ASI and 
actual allocation made to it, to some extent.  
(Para 28.4) 
Lowering the fees charged for filming at Centrally Protected Monuments 
 The Committee does not agree with ASI’s view regarding Rs. 1.00 lakh and Rs. 
50 thousand filming charges being meagre amount s. The Committee is of the view that 

79 
 
films being shot on low budget can find these charges to be prohibitive and thus 
disallow them from featuring our historical monuments and heritage. The Committee, 
therefore, recommends that ASI should review the filming charges presently being 
charged, in light of the prohibitive effect of the same on low -budget movies and the 
opportunity for promotion of historical sites and monuments thus lost by ASI. 
(Para 29.7)
